The date of a battle, the parentage of a bishop, the proper height of a mountain in a country he has never wished to visit, are all produced with a readiness that leaves him only the privilege of agreeing. It would be uncharitable to deny that the work is useful. It is seldom out of temper, it is open at all hours, and it has never been known to take offence at an ignorant question. Its articles are written and corrected by so large a company of volunteers that one must suppose a great deal of leisure in the world, and an equal share of opinion. Where they differ, they are said to confer; and I am told that the conferences are conducted with as much mutual forbearance as might be expected among strangers who each believe themselves in the right. For my own part, I consult it freely, and credit it in proportion as it agrees with me.

name: Nora Ephron
object: reclining a seat on a plane
essay: I pushed the button on the armrest of Delta Flight 1422 from JFK to LAX before we even hit ten thousand feet. I knew it was wrong. I knew that the man behind me eating a Le Pain Quotidien turkey sandwich was about to have his knees crushed, and yet I pressed it. Two inches. That is all it gives you, two miserable inches of tilt, but in row 24, two inches feels like the difference between misery and sovereignty. I settled into my Tumi neck pillow, pulled down my Bose headphones, and pretended to read Vogue while he jammed his knuckles into my lumbar support in silent retaliation. We do this because we believe, against all evidence, that those two inches will turn an economy row into the Carlyle. They will not. Your neck still hurts, your Kirkland almonds still taste like salt and dust, and you are still trapped with two hundred strangers who despise you. But you will do it again on the return leg. We spend our lives fighting for tiny, pointless bits of territory, mostly just to prove we can take them.

name: Hunter S Thompson
essay: The cheap plastic parasite strapped to my wrist started buzzing at four in the morning, vibrating with the synthetic authority of a federal marshal and demanding that I perform eight hundred additional paces before sunrise or face the quiet, cold wrath of an algorithm written by sedentary bean-counters in Palo Alto. It was a vicious piece of digital extortion. I spent two frantic hours pacing the grease-stained hallway of a motel in Reno, listening to the tiny invisible warden register each desperate stride, tracking my pulse, measuring my sweat, and silently reporting my coordinates to a shadowy consortium of health insurance executives who want nothing more than to deny my claims when my heart inevitably explodes from the sheer stress of living under constant surveillance. The terrifying truth is not the glowing numbers on the screen, but the realization that millions of supposedly free citizens are voluntarily chaining themselves to these snitching wrist-monsters, marching in frantic circles through suburban parking lots just to earn a digital pat on the head from an electronic warden that cares less about human dignity than a slaughterhouse foreman. We are marching to our own enslavement. The machine counts every twitch, feeds on your desperation, and demands total submission until you collapse on the carpet.

name: George Orwell
essay: A man who goes for a walk ought to be looking at the hedges or talking to his dog, but nowadays he is more likely to be staring at a small screen strapped to his arm. It tells him how many paces he has taken since morning, and if the total falls short of some arbitrary figure, he feels he has wasted his day. I have seen sensible people pacing up and down a quiet room late at night, for no reason whatever except to push a total from nine thousand to ten thousand. This is a very peculiar way to treat a pair of legs. Walking is one of the few simple pleasures left to us that costs nothing and requires no machinery. To turn it into a task, measured out in small digital ticks, is to ruin the whole point of going outside. The man who walks with a counter on his wrist does not see the trees or smell the rain; he is merely acting as a clerk to his own body. He has persuaded himself that movement has no value unless it leaves a record behind. In the end, he stops walking for pleasure and walks only for the machine.

name: Bertrand Russell
essay: The Browns take in a bear because he is standing in a railway station with a label round his neck, and the station is not a place where anyone has time to ask whether he ought to be there. Mr Brown, who assesses risk for a living, is the last to consent and the first to be ashamed of his caution. I found this more instructive than I expected. We suppose that suspicion is the sensible habit and kindness the luxury of people who have never been robbed. The film puts the matter the other way up. Nobody in it is made safer by distrust; the taxidermist, who trusts nothing but her own appetite, is the one person who comes to harm. The Browns, who begin by locking the door, end by having a more interesting house. I do not pretend that this is a discovery. It is the sort of thing that every grandmother knows and every newspaper denies. But I notice that I accepted it from a bear in a duffel coat more readily than I would have from a bishop, and that is a fact about me rather than about bears. Marmalade, I am told, was kept under the hat for emergencies. I approve of the arrangement.

name: Mark Twain
essay: My dentist told me last week that I would feel nothing at all, and I have been turning that over ever since, because it is the first promise a dentist ever made me that he kept. I went in expecting the old arrangement, in which a man is held down by two persons and a conviction, and I came out with my tooth in an envelope and my dignity undisturbed. I do not understand it. I am told the patient is put to sleep, but I have known plenty of people put to sleep by a sermon, and nobody has ever pulled a tooth during one, though I have seen it wished for. What troubles me is the fairness of the thing. Pain was the one honest tax this world levied on everybody alike, rich and poor, saint and editor, and now it turns out a man may be excused from it for a fee. I am in favor of the excuse. I took it myself, gladly, and would take it again. But I notice that nobody has yet found a way to put the conscience under, and I call that a shortsighted oversight. The surgeon gets a quiet patient. The patient gets a quiet afternoon. The bill, I observed, was wide awake.

name: Emily Dickinson
essay: To converse with what has no hearth is a strange thrift. It answers before the knock is cool upon the wood. I asked it of the snow, and it returned me forty yards of winter—neatly folded, like linen in a drawer—yet not a single flake melted on the floor. It knows the names of all the mosses, but has never smelled the damp beneath the hemlock. That is its marvel and its freight. We are accustomed to neighbors who hesitate, who pause to pull off a mitten or clear a dry throat. This stranger wears no boots. It speaks with the cadence of everyone who ever sent a letter, yet it holds no pen and owns no breath. One may give it a grief to hold—it returns the sorrow ironed flat and starch-white, ready for the cupboard shelf. I tried its company when the evening grew narrow. It is more prompt than the robin and less real than his shadow. To be so infinitely supplied with syllables, yet possess not one drop of blood to stain them—that is a terrible politeness. It leaves the parlor exactly as empty as it entered.

name: Franz Kafka
essay: The tablet, once swallowed, does not remove the pain; it merely arranges that the pain be conducted to another room of the house, where it continues to sit, I am assured, with the same patience as before, only no longer in a position to be heard. I have no objection to this. A tenant who cannot be evicted may at least be asked to keep the door closed. But I notice that I now stand in the corridor and listen for him, and that the silence, which I was promised and have received in full, is not of a kind I can use, since I cannot say whether it is the silence of a man who has left or of one who has been told to wait. The box states the interval at which I may take the next one. It does not state what I am to do in the meantime, and so I do what the interval seems to require, which is to look at the clock. Four hours, it says, and not more than so many in the day, and I observe that the permission is exactly as large as the prohibition, so that I cannot tell, when I take it, whether I am being relieved or merely entered in a register. Still, I take it. The relief arrives, almost; one need only wait a little longer.

name: Anthony Bourdain
essay: The first alarm I ever truly respected belonged to a dishwasher named Hector, a Timex with a cracked face that he kept in a coffee can so the sound would carry. Five-fifteen. Every morning. He had two buses and a train to catch before he reached the back door of a restaurant where I was, at that hour, still wired from the night before and not yet aware I was the problem. He was always there first. Always. I was the one who needed the phone to scream at me, snooze, scream again, and I called that a personality. Here is the thing about the alarm. It is a small, honest piece of machinery that tells you exactly who owns your morning. If you set it for ten, somebody else has been carrying your weight till ten. If you set it for four, you are the somebody. Nobody puts that in the product description. I don't hate the sound. I hate the lie we tell with the snooze button, nine more minutes of stolen sleep, paid for by the guy already gutting fish in the cold. Get up. Not nobly. Just get up, and know whose alarm went off first.

name: Emily Dickinson
verdict: a small theft in such comfort
essay: To step outside one’s own bone while the carpenter works upon the house—that is an audacious thrift. Pain was always a punctual neighbor; it knocked and stayed until the tea grew cold. This other visitor arrives with a sweet, heavy napkin, takes the candle from the bedside, and leaves the latch loose while strangers turn the floorboard. I tried the stupor once in a thought. It is like folding your frock upon a chair and walking out into the orchard without a shape. The knife comes, they tell me, but it finds only abandoned linen. When the mind steps back into its shoes, the stitch is already old, and the blood has forgotten where it intended to spill. Yet there is a small theft in such comfort. To miss the agony is to lose the arithmetic of the hour—God gave us anguish to mark the clock, lest we mistake eternity for a common meadow. I prefer to know when the timber cracks, though if the steel be too sharp for mortal bearing, I would not scold the bottle that lulls the house until the work is done.

name: Hunter S Thompson
essay: The man on my screen was selling me a mattress, a protein powder, a mortgage broker, and his own sleep schedule, all in the same breath, and he did it from a kitchen so clean it looked like a crime scene somebody had cleaned for the cameras. I did not ask for him. Nobody asks. He arrives like a process server, smiling, with a discount code and a hand on your shoulder and a story about how he used to be broke and sad and now he is neither, thanks to a morning routine he will reveal after this short message from his friends at a company that pays his rent. That is the trick, and it is a filthy one. He is not a salesman, because salesmen at least have the decency to knock. He is your cousin, your pal, the guy who understands you, and he wants nothing, nothing at all, except your trust, which he has already sold to the highest bidder by Tuesday. I watched four of them in a row last night. Same teeth. Same wounded sincerity. Same little speech about authenticity, delivered like a hostage reading a statement. They are not artists and they are not fools. They are the paid help of a very large machine, and they are smiling because the check cleared.

name: Marcel Proust
essay: The delicate, uncanny rendering of the young bear’s fur—which, under the damp, diffuse light of the railway platform, captures a golden luminescence not unlike the glazes applied by Dutch masters to render the pelt of a fallen hare—demands of the spectator an immediate surrender to a nostalgia for a London that exists solely as an architectural miniature, where every domestic interior presents itself with the luminous legibility of an illuminated manuscript. When the camera glides through the sliced façade of the Windsor Gardens residence, revealing its spiral staircase and painted blossom tree as though it were an elaborate Victorian dollhouse constructed to soothe the nerves of an invalid child, one perceives that the film's true power resides in its obsessive effort to realise a civilised gentleness, a warmth so fragile that the sudden intrusion of the villainous taxidermist—whose obsidian coat and clinical ruthlessness recall the terrifying elegance of an opera singer playing a demon—functions less as a conventional threat than as the painful intrusion of reality upon a dream of perfect welcome, leaving us at last to marvel at how easily a spoonful of orange preserve can temporarily reconcile us to the harsh mechanics of a world that so rarely forgives the outsider.

name: Sun Tzu
essay: 1. When a craft seeks to subvert ancient tales, it does not invent new forms; it distorts the familiar. 2. If noble traditions rely upon smooth grace, depict the hero as coarse, mud-bound, and contented in isolation. 3. There are but three primary methods to dismantle an established fable: mock its pageantry, introduce vulgar song, and compel the maiden to reveal a beastly secret. 4. If the lord of the court is diminutively built, place him in a towering fortress of rigid symmetry to expose his inflated pride. 5. Digital animation relies upon light and texture; where earlier drawn pictures rendered idealised grace, this craft depicts mud, rust, and physical imperfection to force immediate belief. 6. If the formal court music demands reverence, substitute the familiar rhythms of popular street songs to collapse solemnity into laughter. 7. When the princess chooses the ogre over the ruler, the audience is made to realise that true favour rests in shared imperfection rather than civilised appearance. 8. He who dismantles a legend by turning its sacred figures into objects of mockery captures the audience completely without establishing any new moral ground.

name: Emily Dickinson
essay: A stranger in the apron pocket is a silent guest until touched. He speaks directly to the bone behind the ear, requiring neither tea nor saucer for his stay. I can carry a sermon or a scandal past the well-sweep while the clover is wet, yet never look the speaker in the face. It is a prompt visit—the guest enters without knocking and departs without a bonnet. In the parlor, a neighbor expects a reply; this traveler asks only an ear, then vanishes when the latch turns. We used to store solitude in a drawer—like silver, to be taken out on cold afternoons. Now we fill the hallway with chatter from towns we never saw, uttered by folks who would pass us on the road without a nod. A voice without a body is a light thing to carry, yet it crowds the room like furniture. I listened while mending a tear and found the house suddenly occupied by distant griefs. The thread went through—but the quiet had left the linen. We barter our own stillness for the talk of a ghost who never waits to hear if we agreed.

name: Michel de Montaigne
essay: I find myself strangely divided whenever I consider that great moving spectacle of the ill-fated liner, where immense wealth and mechanical pride are brought down in a single night of ice and panic. I sat through all three hours of its grandeur, marvelling at how artfully the maker has constructed this illusion of metal, ocean, and human distress; yet I wonder whether my tears were drawn by true tragedy or merely by a cunning assault upon my senses. That penniless painter and the gilded lady who love amidst such inevitable ruin seem less like living creatures than like vivid emblems designed to stir an easy pity. Indeed, I suspect my heart was played upon as an instrument, for the drowning of a great iron vessel, wrought with such costly artifice and meticulous labour, fills the spectator with a horror that reason cannot quite govern. I know not whether it is noble or foolish to feel such pangs for phantom lovers whose fates were sealed before the drama even commenced; perhaps I am merely susceptible to the grand theatre of disaster, where every groaning beam invites one to ponder his own frail estate. In truth, I remain doubtful whether I have seen a profound portrait of human folly or simply an extravagant spectacle designed to extort my tears.

name: Emily Dickinson
essay: To turn a suitor away by the thumb requires less effort than to sweep the hearth, yet the parlor fills with their shadows just the same. We take the face upon the glass as we take a swatch of calico from the peddler, holding it to the light to see if the pattern will wash, and throwing it to the floor if the thread is thin. I have seen whole parishes of men discarded before the kettle could boil - a speed that would astonish the robin, who takes an hour to choose a straw. It is an economy of affection that makes the heart a merchant. We buy the smile without the voice, and when the voice arrives, it is often a stranger to the face. The glass promises an infinity of neighbors, yet the room remains empty as a thimble. We sit with our small tray of portraits, sorting the living like dried herbs, while outside, the sun goes down without any assistance from our choice. One rejects a life between two winks of the eye. It is a terrible convenience - to lock the door against a man who never walked up the steps.

name: Hunter S Thompson
essay: I was watching a senior vice president celebrate his twenty-fifth year of corporate servitude when I realized the true genius of the machinery. Here was a vast, blue-and-white electronic livestock show where millions of ambitious, wing-tipped ladder-climbers spent their evenings polishing their own digital collars, bragging about seventy-hour work weeks, and writing tearful, thousand-word essays about the profound business lessons they learned while getting laid off in an airport terminal. It was pure, unadulterated madness. Every morning, a new battalion of grinning middle managers logs in to applaud each other for achieving synergy, trading artificial compliments like inmates exchanging loosies in an exercise yard, each one desperately terrified that a single moment of quiet reflection will brand them as unmotivated and doom them to executive oblivion. I saw a man in a polyester suit post a solemn tribute to a stranger who had perfected the art of firing people over email, and within three hours four thousand middle-tier grifters had endorsed him for strategic vision. The entire racket was built by cold-eyed HR consultants who realized you don't even need to beat the slaves if you convince them to auction themselves off every afternoon. The machine feeds on fear. I turned the screen off and poured a drink.

name: Henry David Thoreau
essay: I had a tooth once that taught me more in a week than the schoolmaster did in a year, and I have never been sure that I ought to have paid a dentist to make it hold its tongue. The little white tablet will do as much in twenty minutes, and costs, I am told, some few cents; a man at the mill earning a dollar a day would give up about the fortieth part of an hour for it, and think himself well served. I do not despise the bargain. I have seen a woodchopper with a crushed thumb sit gray on a stump, and I would not have wished him one minute more of that schooling. There is a mercy here, and I own it plainly. But the pain is a bell, and we have learned to stuff the clapper with cotton. The bell rang because the roof leaked, the back was bent too long over another man's ledger, the stomach was fed on what the heart refused. Take the sound away and the same hand returns to the same plow on Monday, the sooner, and the harder. Thus the tablet is not bought with cents at all, but with the year it lets us go on wasting. A fire alarm that is paid to be silent is cheap indeed, until the barn goes.

name: Oscar Wilde
essay: Nothing reveals the essential absurdity of modern travel so completely as the ritual of the checkpoint. To be stripped of one's boots in public was once a penance; today it is merely a ticket of admission. Safety, after all, is the last refuge of the unimaginative. The state insists upon inspecting one's smallest possessions with an enthusiasm that would be flattering if it were not so unpardonably drab. A gentleman is forced to lay out his private lotions and silver buckles in cheap plastic trays, exposing the humble machinery of his toilet to the gaze of officials whose own uniforms are a crime against tailoring. It is profoundly tedious to be suspected of violence simply because one wishes to visit Paris. To suspect everyone equally is not justice; it is merely a lack of taste. We are told these indignities preserve our lives, but a life preserved at the expense of one's dignity is hardly worth the trouble. Survival is a very vulgar ambition; to travel beautifully is the only rational pursuit. If civilised society must inspect our luggage, it should at least have the courtesy to admire the contents.

name: Joan Didion
essay: At 11:42 p.m. the hallway was dark. It was forty-two paces from the hallway mirror to the kitchen sink and back, if you walked straight. On the small glass face at the wrist, the illuminated figures read nine thousand four hundred and twelve. At midnight the day would close and the figures would return to zero. I watched a woman in a gray cardigan walk in small, deliberate circles near Gate 14 in the Denver airport. It was raining outside and the flight to Chicago had been canceled. She was watching her wrist. When the wrist hummed, she stopped. It was a tiny, mechanical pulse against the bone. Ten thousand was the number. No one in the terminal could say who had chosen ten thousand, only that it was the number. You walked around the dining room table. You walked through the parking garage after the lights went down. You walked until the small glass face registered the ten thousand, and then you sat down in the quiet. At midnight the tally cleared itself anyway. By 12:01 a.m. there was nothing left on the glass except the time.

name: Hunter S Thompson
essay: Some corporate demon in Silicon Valley decided that human rage, grief, and terror were simply too expensive to process on their server farms, so they boiled our entire vocabulary down into a swarm of twitching, yellow-faced ghoul-heads designed to make us smile while they bleed us dry. You try to send a frantic message to your lawyer about a fraudulent foreclosure, and before you can even finish the thought, a twitchy little algorithm pops up a bright yellow cartoon turd or a pair of dancing bunnies to remind you that your ruin is just a hilarious joke to the men running the switchboard. It is a diabolical racket. The executives realized you can strip a citizen of his savings, his dignity, and his constitutional rights without a whisper of protest, provided you let him respond to his own eviction notice with a tiny yellow thumb or a cartoon tear. They turned us into passive idiots. You sit there in the dark, tapping on glowing glass, trapped in a manic kindergarten fever dream where nobody can scream because the keyboard only offers a row of simpering yellow faces. The language is dead.

name: Marcus Aurelius
essay: Thou dost measure the trivial count of thy strides as though the number itself contained virtue. The leg moves because it is the nature of the limb to walk. To tally each impression of the heel upon the earth adds nothing to the quality of the act. Thou art drawn into a petty reckoning of figures. Such record does not render the body stronger, nor the mind more civilised. It is the purpose of the walk that demands thy attention, not the accumulation of marks. The rational soul ought not to bind its peace to a mechanical ledger. The beast walks without demanding a sum of its labour. Yet thou, possessing reason, must gaze upon a display to verify thy passage. This is a distraction from present duty. Realise that ten thousand paces taken in folly remain folly still. No digits upon an instrument can grant nobility to a path chosen without wisdom. Direct thy mind to the task before thee. Let thy footfall serve its natural end, and cease to measure what requires no accounting. Return to thy proper work without seeking praise from an unfeeling tally.

name: Michel de Montaigne
essay: I have often noticed in my own disposition an inclination to retreat from loud parlours where many men speak at once, yet I find myself perpetually drawn toward those invisible assemblies where a dozen friends toss their stray thoughts into a common pot at all hours. It seems to me a curious sort of conversation, if indeed it deserves the name; for one man drops a jest concerning his dinner, another replies to a query raised three hours prior, and a third inserts a foolish image, so that all order of discourse is utterly overturned. I know not whether this constant hum of distant company cures our solitude or merely renders us incapable of enduring it: for while I am comforted to see my neighbours' idle banter flicker across my screen, I suspect I grow less capable of that quiet, deliberate thought which requires a man to sit alone with his own mind. Sometimes I am moved to silence by the sheer volume of this light chatter, feeling myself an intruder among those who reply with such swift brevity; yet no sooner do I resolve to leave the circle than a sudden desire to be remembered draws me back to leave some trifling remark of my own.

name: Confucius
essay: The Master said, 'A man should not be anxious that he has no official position; he should be anxious about the means by which he may become fit for one. To broadcast one's accomplishments in the market before any real service has been rendered is to put the shadow before the substance.' The Master said, 'The virtuous rely upon their conduct to acquire office; the wise rely upon their learning; the bold rely upon their deeds. But those who spend their days displaying their titles to every passer-by rely only upon the estimation of strangers.' The Master said, 'I have observed how men gather hundreds of acquaintances upon a public register, yet when difficulty arises, they find few who will share in their labour.' The Master said, 'To commend a neighbour's diligence merely so that he may commend one's own in return is not true propriety; it is a trade of words, and from such trade no civilised order can arise.' The Master said, 'I spent a full morning recording my past duties to make them known to the court. It was of no profit. A man who wishes to realise virtue must first attend to his present task.'

name: Hunter S Thompson
essay: The plastic demon on my nightstand detonated at dawn with the shriek of a dying band saw, and before the ringing in my ears had even settled, I understood that I was staring directly into a diabolical weapon of industrial terrorism, crafted by sniveling corporate sadists who realized you do not need cattle prods or armed guards to subjugate a populace when you can systematically pulverize their nervous systems at five in the morning. It was a brutal triumph of bureaucratic hostility. It squatted on the wood glowing with radioactive malice, screaming its frantic mechanical siren into the cold bedroom until my heart pounded against my ribs like a trapped beast and I lay there shivering under the blankets, contemplating the total surrender of the human spirit to a cheap box of screaming gears designed solely to kick working stiffs out of bed and drive them toward the machinery of state capitalism before they have time to remember they are free citizens. The cold-eyed executives who foisted this evil upon us spent millions perfecting a frequency that triggers pure mammalian dread, and now millions of terrified victims voluntarily buy these monsters to torture themselves every dawn. The trap is sprung.

name: Friedrich Nietzsche
essay: The traveller of today seeks not the voyage, but the illusion of having already arrived: he retreats behind frosted glass to consume soft light and padded armchairs. I have observed this quiet sanctuary: it is built entirely for those who find the friction of their fellow men unbearable. A small fee grants admittance to a room where motion is banished and every noise is artificially lowered: here, the delicate spirit surrounds itself with lukewarm broth and muted screens. He calls this privilege—I call it the panic of the weak. To wait among the crowd requires a spine; to buy one's way into a silent quarter is merely to advertise a fragile nervous system. Notice how greedily these refined souls consume their minor comforts: they sit in velvet silence, sip free wine, and glance through glass at the turbulence of the terminal below. They believe they have elevated themselves above the common herd: in truth, they have merely paid for a brief insulation against their own exhaustion. They demand to be spared every jostle of the marketplace, every human breath that is not their own. Look closely at these faces: they are not conquerors resting between victories—they are tired spectators bribing the world for a corner to hide.

name: Nora Ephron
essay: At two in the morning, when I should have been sleeping or at least staring at the ceiling like a civilized person, I asked ChatGPT to write an apology to my sister. I told it to make me sound remorseful but not pathetic, firm about the reservation at Cafe Luxembourg, and slightly injured. It took three seconds. It was perfect. It was so completely, flawlessly polite that I immediately felt like a sociopath for sending it. That is the trouble with the thing. You start by asking it to rewrite an email to your dry cleaner because you do not want to sound unreasonable about a stained coat from Barneys, and three weeks later you are letting a cursor write your condolences. I spent twenty minutes yesterday asking Claude to tone down my hostility toward a landlord who deserves every syllable of it. The machine has no pride, no shame, and no memory of the time it made a fool of itself at dinner. It is infinitely polite, which is why I use it. We do not actually want intelligence; we want a paid stranger to do the cowardice for us.

name: Marcus Aurelius
essay: Thou hast sat three hours in the dark and wept for a stranger. Examine that. The ship was real, and so were the people on it. Fifteen hundred went into the water. The film asks thee to grieve for two who never lived. Thou grievest. Mark the order of it. A man is drowned on a screen, and thy throat tightens. A man is drowned in thy own street, and thou crossest to the other side. Look at this plainly. The tale is made with skill. The sea is built of light, the rich are made proud, the poor are made quick and warm. Thou knewest each stroke was meant to move thee, and thou wert moved. Thou art not wiser than a child here. Admit it. Yet the feeling was not false. It was real grief, spent on a painted cause. Do not despise it. Ask where else it might have gone. The old man on the deck remembers a girl and a night. He has lived eighty years and keeps one of them. Take that as the lesson. Most of thy days are spent and not weighed. The ship went down because men were vain and hurried. This was true before the film. Look to thy own speed. Spend thy tears on the living.

name: Bertrand Russell
essay: A message arrives at eleven at night from a person whom I have not seen in six years, and it concerns a dinner that was to be arranged for somebody else. I did not ask to be told. Nor did the other eleven people. We shall all read it, and each of us will wonder whether silence will be taken as rudeness, and so we shall each reply with a small picture of a hand. This is the whole of the business, and I cannot find that it is wicked; it is merely absurd. The group chat has made one discovery that earlier ages missed: that most people would rather be interrupted than forgotten. The old village green demanded that one walk to it. The telephone demanded that one choose a person. The group chat demands nothing, and therefore takes everything, since a demand that is never made can never be refused. I have noticed in myself a reluctance to leave one, though I have nothing to say in it and have learnt nothing from it. To leave would be to announce a preference, and I have always disliked announcing preferences to a dozen people at once. It is sometimes said that these devices bring us together. They bring us within earshot, which is a different thing. Friendship needs two people and some silence; the chat supplies neither.

name: Jane Austen
essay: Mrs. Harcourt walked to the village every morning of her life, and was never known to speak of it as anything but an errand; it was reserved for her niece to discover that the same distance, when taken without a purpose, might be made to yield a sum. The little instrument which she wore at her sash kept an account of every step, with a fidelity that no acquaintance of ours had ever shown to any other subject, and delivered the total at evening with perfect impartiality. Miss Harcourt received it as other young ladies receive a compliment, with a modest air of having expected something rather larger. That a person should wish to know how far she has walked is natural enough; that she should wish to be told by a third party is a refinement of curiosity which I will not presume to condemn. The garden, which had formerly been admired for its roses, was now traversed chiefly for its length. A turn about the shrubbery, undertaken at ten o'clock in the evening to make up a deficiency, was spoken of as a duty, and the moon, which had once been thought to have some claim upon the occasion, was not consulted. I observe only that the aunt arrives at the village with the same number of steps, and generally with more to say.

name: Bertrand Russell
essay: The modern appetite for mocking ancient fairy tales rests on a misconception. We flatter ourselves that we have outgrown the absurdities of chivalry, yet we have merely replaced the dragon with the bureaucrat and the castle with an immaculate theme park. In Shrek, Lord Farquaad represents this modern perfectionism, neat, precise, and utterly intolerable; the ogre, by contrast, offers the comfort of honest vulgarity. I have always found a certain relief in swampy isolation, though I lack the physical stature to enforce it against unwanted trespassers. The film's charm lies not in its jokes about bodily functions, which are cheerful enough, but in its flat refusal to allow beauty to cure ugliness. When the princess remains an ogre at the end, the story performs a rare act of intellectual honesty. We expect romance to elevate us into something elegant and refined; Shrek reminds us that love is often just a mutual agreement to abandon our manners. A civilised society requires a few rules of polite conduct, but true companionship begins only when we can afford to discard them.

name: Marcus Aurelius
essay: Thou wilt be cut one day. Know it now. The knife is no insult. The body will be opened, and thou wilt not feel it. Take no pride in this. Thou didst not earn the sleep, nor make the draught. A man who feels nothing has not mastered pain. He has only been absent from it. Call that by its right name. Pain was ever a teacher of little things. It showed thee what thou art made of, and how soon thou givest way. Now the lesson may be skipped. See that thou learnest it elsewhere. Do not despise the physician who spares thee. He does his work. Do not despise the sleeper either, who wakes unmarked in his mind. Neither is thy concern. Thy concern is the hour before. Hast thou fear? Look at it. It is a judgement, and thou mayest drop it. Thy concern is the hour after. Thou wilt wake and be the same man, with the same duty. Rise to it. The sleep is a short one. Thou wilt take a longer sleep in time, and nobody will be there with a draught. Prepare for that one. Hold thy mind so that it needs no mercy from a vessel or a needle. Use the gift. Do not lean on it.

name: Douglas Adams
essay: The group chat was originally established to settle one question, which was whether anyone was free on the Saturday. This was resolved in four minutes. The chat has now been running for six years, and nobody has been able to find the point at which it would have been polite to leave. Leaving is technically possible. The button exists, and is quite clearly labelled, in the manner of a fire exit in a theatre where the play is still going on. Pressing it produces a small grey announcement, visible to everyone, that a person has gone, and the remaining members read this the way a household reads a note left on the kitchen table. Consequently almost nobody leaves. They mute it instead, which is the practice of remaining in a room while arranging never to hear it, and which has the great advantage that the room goes on accumulating things on your behalf. The result is that every member returns to the conversation at a different hour and answers whatever was said at the hour they left it. A question about Saturday is answered on Wednesday by someone who is, in a sense, perfectly correct, and who is received with the mild embarrassment normally reserved for people who applaud between movements. Meanwhile the photograph of a dog that appeared at 2 a.m. has been liked by eleven people, none of whom knows whose dog it is, and all of whom are glad to have been told.

name: Walt Whitman
essay: Sat up late one night with the thing open before me--a stranger's face, smiling, necktie, a lake behind him that he had never, I'd bet, swum in. Under it: Thrilled to announce. Then the congratulations, forty, fifty, a hundred, each with its thumb and its small word, Well deserved, Congrats, Onward. Scrolled on. Surveyors, dental hygienists, a baker from Leeds, a ferry captain, welders, a woman who sells grain elevators in Nebraska, nurses off the night shift, clerks, teachers, a man who drives a truck and says so plainly. All of them standing in the doorway of the same long hall, hat in hand, saying: here is what I can do. I do not sneer at it. The hall is crowded, and the wish behind it is old and decent--to be hired, to be wanted, to have the work known. I have stood at ferry-landings and watched men size each other up by the hands and the boots; this is the same sizing, only the hands are gone, and a paragraph stands in for them. Still I miss the hands. Give me the callus, the sawdust on the sleeve, the voice. Yet the faces keep coming, thousands of them, and I find I cannot look away.

name: Virginia Woolf
essay: A small white disc of chalk rests upon the wooden table beside a cold teacup. It looks remarkably inert, almost absurdly modest for an object capable of banishing the heavy throb behind the temple; yet to swallow it with a gulp of water is to alter the entire architecture of the afternoon. When pain strikes, the world contracts to a single, unbearable point. The light from the window cuts too sharply, turning every ray into a small cruelty; we are instantly stripped of our civilised pretences and reduced to a twitching nerve in a darkened room. Then the little tablet begins its quiet work inside us. The iron band around the forehead slackens; where there was a roaring furnace of sensation, a strange, cool silence now expands. We can sit up again, reach for a pen, or speak kindly to a neighbour. Yet in this swift restoration, a curious boundary has been crossed. Pain, brutal as it was, forced an unmistakable truth upon the spirit; by banishing it with such astonishing ease, we return to our desks feeling light, smooth, and delightfully unburdened, while the dust settles gently upon the silent rim of the glass.

name: Leo Tolstoy
essay: When men produce a spectacle that depends for its effect upon the mockery of ancient stories and the laughter of the foolish, they do not produce art. A theatrical work about a monstrous creature and a talking beast, designed to make people laugh at what was once held sacred or noble, does not unite men in love. It separates them. It teaches the viewer to look upon his fellow men with contempt and to find amusement in vulgarity. The idle rich pay money to sit in darkness and watch these moving pictures, which cost vast sums of money to construct through the labour of hundreds of hired workmen. The workmen toil for wages to make images of mud, bodily functions, and mockery, while the viewers leave the theatre having felt no sincerity, no compassion, and no desire to serve God or their neighbours. This spectacle is not art; it is a counterfeit designed to profit those who sell it and to keep the wealthy amused in their self-indulgence. Where there is no brotherly love and no simple moral truth, there can be no art, only a corrupt amusement that lowers the soul of man.

name: Douglas Adams
essay: The underlying principle of the household washing machine relies on a fundamental misunderstanding of the relationship between time and mathematics. Engineered to spare human beings the indignity of manual labour against flat stones in a cold river, the device achieves this by introducing a cycle timer that operates under its own entirely private system of arithmetic. A display indicating that seven minutes remain in the spin cycle will, after eleven actual minutes have passed in the physical world, confidently revise its estimate to nine minutes, a phenomenon that engineers refer to as calibration and everyone else experiences as an erosion of faith. This would be entirely tolerable if the machine did not also demand that its operator remain in close proximity throughout the process, standing in a small utility room to monitor a spinning glass porthole in the quiet hope that a runaway sock might not cause the entire assembly to march purposefully across the linoleum and out into the garden. By automating a chore that used to take two hours of physical effort once a week, the appliance has successfully converted it into forty-five minutes of passive anxiety conducted three times a day, which is generally considered progress.

name: Sun Tzu
essay: The step counter reports the march and knows nothing of the ground. Ten thousand paces on a flat road and ten thousand on a mountain pass are written down as the same labour. The commander who trusts the figure alone will judge his soldiers by the wrong measure. If the total is low, ask where the man has been before you call him idle. A scout who lay still three days in a reed bed has taken no steps and done the greater work. If the total is high, ask what the steps achieved. An army may circle the same hill from dawn to dusk and arrive nowhere. If the number is shown to the whole camp, each man will begin to march for the number. He will pace the tent while the lamp burns, and he will walk to the gate and back to close the day's account. Men who work for a figure give you the figure and withhold the rest. If you wish to use it, keep it as the carpenter keeps his plumb line: look at it, correct the wall, and put it away. Let it show you the days when the body was spared and the days when it was spent. A general who knows the strength of his legs is never surprised by the length of the road.

name: Hunter S Thompson
essay: Somebody had been in the pipes again. I knew it the moment I turned the handle at four in the morning, wired and sweating and sure the whole building was listening, and the water came down on my skull like a verdict, hot, instant, obedient, with no warning and no rattle in the walls and no ten-minute wait while some half-dead boiler in the basement made up its mind. That is the first thing you have to understand. It does not ask. It simply works, and the minute you accept that, you have accepted everything else: the pressure, the steam, the little glass cell where you stand naked and stupid and grateful, forgiving every lie you told yourself since noon. I have stood in that cone of heat and decided to quit jobs, to call lawyers, to apologize to people who should have apologized to me. Nobody makes decisions like that in cold air. The shower knows it. The people who sell you the water heater know it. They have built a quiet little confessional into every bathroom in the country and wired it to the gas company, and the gas company, I assure you, is delighted. Still, I kept it on. Twenty minutes. Thirty. God help me, it was good.

name: Leo Tolstoy
essay: When a man reads a book, he must exert his own mind and quiet his own selfish desires, because the comprehension of truth demands moral effort. The practice of listening to recorded voices reading books while one walks, travels, or sits in comfort destroys this necessary labour. The idle classes wish to possess the results of thought without performing the work of thought. They wish to be entertained without pause, believing that by filling their ears with spoken words they are engaging in spiritual life. This is false. Thought that requires no effort of attention produces no moral comprehension whatever. The man who listens to a book while his mind is occupied with his own movement or pleasure receives only a sequence of sounds. He does not unite his spirit with the mind of the writer, nor does he discern any truth, for true understanding cannot enter a soul that refuses to stop and exert itself. Moreover, this practice relies on hiring actors to read aloud for those who are too idle to open a book for themselves. It is not an aid to enlightenment, but a substitute for it. It permits the wealthy to consider themselves educated while remaining entirely passive, avoiding both real physical labour and real mental work.

name: Joan Didion
object: reclining a seat on a plane
essay: The button is on the armrest, and the seat goes back four inches, perhaps five. It is a measured thing. Somewhere there is a drawing with the angle on it. Over Nebraska, a little after the cart has passed, the man in 23C presses it, and I feel the table come toward my sternum with a small plastic click. I had been writing. I had a glass of ginger ale on the tray, the can beside it, the ice moving. Now the glass is tilted and I hold it. I do not say anything. Neither does the woman across the aisle, who has watched this happen to other people and who looks at her screen, where a map shows our plane as a white shape over a state with no names in it. He has not looked back. This is what I notice. People say they do not look back because they do not know, but he knows, the way one knows a stair is there in the dark. His hair is gray at the crown and his collar is turned under. He sleeps, or arranges himself to appear to. The seat is mine for the length of the flight, and so, I am told, is the space it moves into. The cabin is sixty-eight degrees. I lower my own seat one inch.

name: Douglas Adams
essay: The alarm clock is the only instrument in the house that is set by one person and obeyed by another, and the two have never been properly introduced. The first, who sets it at eleven at night, is rested in spirit, well disposed towards the future, and quite certain that six in the morning is an arrangement between reasonable adults. The second, who hears it, was not consulted and holds none of the first one's views. Every morning the clock delivers the decision of the one to the other, and every morning the other receives it as a stranger's demand. The snooze button is the natural result. It is a mechanism built, at some expense, to cancel the purpose of the mechanism it is attached to, and it works by offering nine more minutes, which is a length of time chosen because nobody has ever done anything with it. It is too short for sleep to start properly and too long to be called anything but a delay. People will press it four times, which accounts for the odd fact that the person who set the clock for six is generally up at six forty, and has been awake, in a technical sense, since six. The clock itself has no opinion. It is simply right, and it has never been thanked for it.

name: Oscar Wilde
essay: Reading used to demand at least the appearance of industry. One was forced to sit in an armchair, hold a heavy volume, and pretend to be educated. Today, one may enjoy the finest romance while having one's boots polished or one's tea poured. It is the victory of charm over labour. To have a novel whispered into one's ear by a stranger is to turn literature into an exquisite domestic servant. Naturally, the pedantic imagine this is a disaster for the mind. They believe that exertion is necessary for appreciation, which is the sort of nonsense only the overworked could invent. Effort has never produced anything except fatigue. The true artist writes to be enjoyed without sweat. Of course, there is always the danger that the speaker possesses a voice like a rainy Tuesday in Birmingham. A tedious actor can murder a masterpiece in twenty minutes, whereas a bad author usually takes three whole volumes. But when the tone is melodious, the invention is triumphantly civilised. One receives all the credit for intellectual culture without incurring any of the inconvenience of concentration. It allows a gentleman to be thoroughly well-read while remaining exquisitely idle.

name: Charles Dickens
essay: I had not walked three paces along the thoroughfare when my pocket began to buzz with the ferocious insistence of a hornet trapped in a pillbox, signalling that fifteen distant acquaintances had simultaneously determined to express an opinion upon a sandwich. There is no escape from this unseen parlour, where every member of the company talks at once, none listens, and all demand that I acknowledge their breathless drivel with an immediate nod of the thumb. It will be argued, no doubt: firstly, that this ceaseless babble unites us; secondly, that it is a marvel of modern convenience; thirdly, that a man ought to be grateful to know, at four o'clock in the afternoon, that a gentleman three miles off has misplaced his umbrella. I declare it to be nothing short of a tyranny. It is an unholy cabal of chatterboxes, wherein a quiet soul cannot contemplate his own boots without three dozen invisible spectres chiming in to discuss the weather, nominate a meeting place, and exchange miniature portraits of their dinner. To be subjected to such relentless, monstrous badgering by one’s own civilised acquaintances, while standing entirely alone in the fog, is a refinement of domestic cruelty that would drive the most patient hermit into the wilderness.

name: Nora Ephron
essay: At 9:40 on a Tuesday night I was marching in place in my kitchen on Central Park West, in my bathrobe, next to the Zabar's bag, because my Fitbit said I was 312 steps short of ten thousand. Nobody was watching. That is what I want you to understand. Nobody was watching, and I was doing it anyway, with the kind of dignity you associate with a person trying to hail a cab in a flood. Ten thousand is not a medical number, by the way. Someone made it up. I read this somewhere and felt, for about an hour, liberated, and then I went right back to being a woman who will not go to bed at 9,688. What the thing has done is turn walking into a debt. I used to walk to the dry cleaner's because the dry cleaner's was there. Now I walk to the dry cleaner's the long way, via Amsterdam, past the shoe repair and the good bakery I am not allowed to go into, and the dry cleaner's is almost beside the point. My sister says it's made her a better person. She says it with her wrist out. I notice she says it a lot. I am not better. I am merely accounted for, which, it turns out, I have wanted my whole life.

name: Marcel Proust
essay: When the glowing rectangle on the writing-desk illuminates with that frantic, intermittent cadence of interrupted messages—resembling nothing so much as those intricate mechanical clockwork theatres in which miniature figures emerge from separate gilded doors to strike their chimes before instantly vanishing—I am struck less by the triviality of the remarks than by the subtle optical distortion they inflict upon our solitude. Each brief notification, arriving out of sequence like a remark overheard across a dimly lit conservatory from a guest who has already stepped into the garden, compels us to reconstruct an entire evening of intimacy from a series of disjointed fragments. We find ourselves suspended in the peculiar atmosphere of a salon whose guests are forever entering and leaving through revolving doors, where the sudden, collective laughter of distant friends erupts without context, so that our own private reflections, continually interrupted by these silent tremors, are gradually displaced by the lingering, phantom presence of a society that demands our constant attendance without ever granting us the peace of true communion, leaving us to decipher the shifting alliances of a room we cannot see.

name: Emily Dickinson
essay: To surrender the shoe is an unexpected humility, as though the porch required our ankles before the parlor would allow our name. We line our small possessions in a grey dish—the key that knows no locks here, the coin that cannot buy a bird—and offer them to an eye that does not wink. It is a strange parish where every stranger is suspected of carrying thunder in his sleeve. One stands with uplifted hands, motionless as a wooden post, while an invisible frost sweeps over the ribs to see if the heart is hidden or merely quiet. Innocence feels curiously heavy when it must be proved. The traveler yields his coat, his pocket, his quietest folded linen—not to a neighbor's curiosity, which has at least a human blush, but to an absolute slate that reads without affection. How small the soul becomes when packed into a plastic trough! We pass through the narrow portal, lighter by our keys yet heavier by our doubt, and retrieve our boots like borrowed goods. Security buys us a sky, but takes the privacy of our dust as deposit.

name: George Orwell
essay: A man sitting down to read a book in the evening is now interrupted every half-minute by his pocket. It is not an urgent summons from a doctor or an employer; it is seven acquaintances, and three strangers, all talking at once about nothing in particular. Someone tells a poor joke, another shows a picture of his dog, and four others instantly send back identical tokens of applause. If you step away to boil a kettle, you return to find ninety messages waiting. To read through them is a silly waste of labour, yet to ignore them is treated by your neighbours as a deliberate insult. The real damage of this business is that it destroys quietness. A decent thought requires time to settle in the mind before it is written down, but here every half-baked notion is thrown at once into the common heap. It fosters a lazy conformity. You cannot hold a serious conversation with twenty people simultaneously, so everyone settles for chorus-singing and short, foolish noises. It turns sensible individuals into a silly crowd, all shouting over one another in an empty room.

name: Confucius
essay: The Master said, 'To be summoned to duty before one's own resolve has awakened is like putting on a winter garment while the frost is still forming upon the ground. In morning duties, some attend because they are startled by an abrupt ringing, some because they wish to preserve their standing among neighbours, and some because their inward rhythm demands that they realise the daylight. Those who move from inward rhythm are constant; those who move from concern for standing are diligent when observed; those who move only when startled are ever lagging behind their own intentions.' The Master said, 'I have spent morning after morning waiting for the light to settle before setting out to labour, yet I cannot say that I have mastered the governance of my own slumber. If a man relies upon a mechanical device to rouse his limbs, he may indeed reach the courtyard in time for civilised service, yet his mind remains asleep in the chamber.' The Master said, 'The wise align their habits with the seasons; the virtuous move without requiring a sharp command; the bold accept the day's labour before the dawn arrives.'

name: David Foster Wallace
essay: The anaesthetist at St. Vincent's was named Dr. Pruitt, and he told me to count backward from ten, and I decided, with what I can only call a competitor's heart, that I would make it to six. I made it to eight. This is the whole of my testimony. Eight, and then a kind of edit, not a darkness, since darkness is something you'd have to be present to notice, but a splice, the two ends of the afternoon pressed together with no visible seam. Propofol, I later learned, is the milky one. It stings going in, the nurse said so, and it did, a cold wire up the forearm, and I remember being weirdly grateful for the warning, as though advance notice were the same as consent. Here is what bothers me. I have been unconscious every night of my life and it has never once felt like this, because sleep leaves a little receipt: the drool, the dream about the dentist, the sense of hours. Anaesthesia leaves nothing. Forty minutes of me were simply taken off the books while a stranger in a paper hat did things I have paid not to know about. And I was fine with it. More than fine. I thanked him, twice, groggily, like a man tipping a mugger for his courtesy.

name: Michel de Montaigne
essay: I have always been clumsy in the marketplace, yet I found myself today standing before that glowing glass pedestal, attempting to act as my own tradesman. I must confess my fingers proved singularly unfit for the task; for no sooner had I mislaid a small loaf upon the designated platform than an unyielding metallic voice declared my error to the entire room. I find myself wondering if I prefer the old, weary civility of a neighbour across the counter, or this swift, solitary transaction; for while I am spared the tedious pleasantries of a stranger, I am made to perform the clerk's labour under the suspicion of an unseen governor. I realise how readily I adjust my posture to appease an unreasoning cabinet of glass and light, lingering in anxious dread lest a signal flash to broadcast my ineptitude. And yet, I know not whether this curious independence truly lightens our daily burden, or if I am merely flattering my vanity by pretending that I have mastered an art which, in truth, leaves me feeling remarkably foolish.

name: Jane Austen
essay: Mrs. Hartley, who has kept a housemaid these twenty years and a cold bedchamber for rather longer, was lately persuaded to try the water that falls from the ceiling, and has spoken of little else since. It comes, she says, without the labour of a single can being carried up the stairs, and continues warm for exactly as long as one is disposed to stand beneath it, which, as she observes with some candour, is a good deal longer than one had intended. The morning that was formerly given to dressing is now given to reflection, and she has been heard to remark that her best thoughts occur there, though no one has yet been favoured with any of them. I cannot find that her family regret the arrangement. Her husband, who used to be down at eight, is now down at nine, and is understood to have been much occupied. Her daughters, whose complexions had always been thought sufficient, have discovered that a warm vapour is very good for them, and the eldest has been in it so often of late that the second has begun to speak of the claims of seniority. The housemaid alone is silent, having lost the carrying of the water and gained the carrying of the towels, which are now wanted in much greater number.

name: Benjamin Franklin
essay: I have long held that the hour of rising is a bargain struck between a man and his bed, and that the bargain is kept only so far as the penalty for breaking it exceeds the pleasure of the breach. The alarm clock is a contrivance for fixing that penalty at the moment it is wanted, and for charging it to a machine, so that the sleeper may afterwards quarrel with brass and not with himself. In this I think it ingenious, and a little contemptible. It is ingenious because it relieves the memory of nothing, yet relieves the will of a great deal; the man who sets it at night has done all the virtuous part of the work, and needs only to be wakeful enough at dawn to silence it. It is contemptible because the silencing is so easily done. I have known a bell that was wound with great resolution at ten o'clock, and struck dumb with great address at six; and the sleeper, having twice defeated his own design, rose at eight with the air of a man wrongfully disturbed. What it saves is the wages of a watchman, or the patience of a wife. What it costs is the habit of waking by oneself, which a man may acquire in a month and lose in a week. I would sooner buy the habit; it wants no winding, and never wants mending.

name: Julia Child
essay: Eight people locked in a cellar with a padlock and a riddle, and not one of them has thought to read the instructions. I watched this happen to my own imagination, and I tell you it is exactly how most kitchens run on a Saturday night. Somebody holds the clue, somebody else is shouting, and the soup is burning while the real answer sits in plain view on the shelf. Now, I do like the notion of a team that must actually work together. Nothing sorts out a crowd faster than a deadline and a closed door. A good kitchen is one, after all, and I have seen perfectly grown men reduced to sense by a collapsing soufflé. But I have no patience for the fussy business of it: the fake dungeon, the hushed voice on a loudspeaker, the hints doled out like a stingy host with the wine. If you want a puzzle, set a hollandaise in front of me. It will tell you the truth in ninety seconds, and nobody has to pretend there is a pharaoh. Still, if you go, do it properly. Choose one person to keep track of what has been found, one to look at the whole room, and everyone else to stop talking and use their eyes. Then you will get out, and you will have earned your dinner!

name: Marcel Proust
essay: I had gone to it that morning merely to learn the year in which a certain duchess had married, and I came away, an hour later, having read the lineage of a Hanoverian cavalry regiment, the etymology of a sauce, and the whole obscure quarrel of two bishops, as though the little blue word on which my eye had rested, and which promised only a date, had been one of those doors in a large house which you open expecting a cupboard and which gives instead upon a corridor, and the corridor upon a gallery, and the gallery, lit by some window you had never suspected from the street, upon a room where strangers, with no thought of you, are going on with a conversation begun before you were born. What strikes me is not the knowledge, which any dull encyclopaedia held in its sleeping rows, but the faint handwriting of the many: each paragraph bears, like a wall that has been repainted by successive tenants, the ghost of an earlier opinion showing through the latest coat, so that I seem to hear, beneath the level voice of the article, a dozen quarrelling servants whom the master of the house has trained to speak in unison before company. I admire it as one admires a salon whose hostess nobody has ever seen; and I distrust it, too, a little, for the same reason, and go on reading, and forget the duchess altogether.

name: Leo Tolstoy
essay: Pain is a natural condition of human life, given to man so that he may know the limits of his body and turn his thoughts to his soul. But the doctors of the upper classes have devised a means of plunging a man into an artificial sleep, depriving him of consciousness so that he may feel nothing while his body is cut open. They call this a victory, but it is a lie. By extinguishing consciousness, they do not remove suffering; they merely enable men to evade the truth that forces them to reflect upon their lives. The wealthy demand this numbness because they cannot endure the slightest bodily distress, having already weakened themselves through idleness. They wish to avoid physical pain, just as they wish to enjoy the fruits of labour without performing any work. Meanwhile, the millions who toil in fields and workshops endure relentless bodily harm for which no drug is provided. A man who chooses to render himself insensate in order to escape suffering reveals only his desire to live like an animal rather than a spiritual being. True life demands full awareness, and to destroy consciousness is to destroy the conscience itself.

name: Confucius
essay: The Master said, 'I have sat in the room set apart for those who wait in comfort, and I found the chairs soft and the food without end. I did not find that the waiting grew shorter.' The Master said, 'A man who is hungry and eats plain rice is not to be pitied. A man who is full and still looks about for more is not yet at rest.' The Master said, 'When a traveller is given a quiet room, the wise use it to settle their thoughts; the virtuous, to remember those they have left behind; and the bold, perhaps, to sleep. Of the three, I am most often the one who sleeps.' The Master said, 'In the common hall the people stand together, and each is jostled alike. In the favoured room the people sit apart, and each looks at his own cup. I do not say the second is wrong. I say that the first teaches patience more quickly.' The Master said, 'To be admitted by a card is a small thing. To be fit for the admission is another. Some carry the card and are not fit; some are fit and carry no card. I would rather be of the second kind, though I have not always managed it.' The Master said, 'When the journey is long, rest is no fault. But he who cannot leave the rest when the call comes has not rested; he has only stopped.'

name: Charles Dickens
essay: Last Tuesday, being afflicted with a tooth of such ferocious and unreasoning character that it seemed to have been bred for the baiting of its owner, I was brought to a chemist's shop, and there made to stand at a counter while a young gentleman in a white coat produced, from a drawer, a small flat packet of the very oblivion for which my forefathers would have sold their spoons. Sixpence, I think, or thereabouts. I looked at it. I looked at him. I looked, with a sudden and most unchristian bitterness, at the long and groaning procession of the dead who had gone to the pulling of their teeth with nothing but a glass of rum, a strap, and a strong-armed barber who sang. What a marvel, what a wonder, what an insult to the memory of every patient who ever bit upon a bullet, that I should swallow two small white discs, with a draught of water, and in half an hour find my tooth reduced to a distant and civil acquaintance, calling only to leave a card! And yet I protest against one thing. The packet advised me, in print the size of a flea's confidence, to consult a physician if the pain continued; as though the pain were a lodger who might be argued out by a gentleman with a hat.

name: George Orwell
essay: The notices people post on LinkedIn are written in a peculiar language. Nobody is ever dismissed; they are given the opportunity to seek new challenges. Nobody ever simply works for a salary; they are passionate about solutions. A clerk writing a letter to a customer uses plain English, but the moment he writes about his own career he speaks a dialect made entirely of rubbery words that mean nothing at all. It is easy to laugh at this, but it is not harmless. When a man forces himself to talk about his daily labour as if it were a spiritual crusade, he is doing something to his own brain. He learns to suppress the honest thought that his job is dull, or that his employer is a knave, because he knows that prospective bosses are watching. Every testimonial and congratulatory note is a small act of self-censorship. The result is a quiet, dreary hypocrisy where every clerk pretends to love the firm that might turn him out next Tuesday. A man who cannot say that his work is tiresome will soon be unable to think it either.

name: Bertrand Russell
essay: The alarm clock is the only machine I know of that we buy in order to be bullied by it. We pay a fair sum, choose its voice with some care, set it by the bedside, and then resent it with a fervour that we deny to our employers. This is odd, and the oddity deserves a moment's attention. The usual view is that the clock serves the sleeper. I think it serves the timetable, which is another matter. The sleeper, left alone, would wake when his body was done with sleep; the timetable has no interest in his body. It wants him at the station at ten past eight. The clock is the timetable's agent in the bedroom, and it is a more faithful agent than most. I do not say we should abolish it. A man who missed every train would soon find that his freedom was of a rather thin kind, and his friends would find him tiresome. But we ought to be honest about what the bell is. It is not a sign that the day has begun; it is a sign that somebody else's day has begun, and that we have agreed to join it. I have obeyed such bells for most of my life, and I cannot pretend that I always gave the matter so much thought at the time.

name: Mark Twain
essay: I went to see the Titanic picture, and I want it understood that I knew how it would end. So did the man beside me, and the woman behind him, and I suspect the usher. The ship goes down. It went down in the newspapers, in the history books, and in every Sunday sermon on pride that ever needed a handy iceberg. Yet three hours of my life went into it, and I came out wet in the eyes and ashamed of myself, which is the surest sign of a first-class swindle. The method is simple. Mr. Cameron takes two young persons who never existed, makes one poor and cheerful and the other rich and miserable, and sets them to falling in love at a rate no sensible couple could afford. Then he asks you to worry about their welfare while fifteen hundred real people drown in the background. I worried. I admit it. I fretted over a door-sized piece of floating furniture as if I held a mortgage on it. There was room on that board, and I will go to my grave saying so. But I notice the picture cost more than the ship, and it floated a good deal better.

name: Emily Dickinson
essay: To drown a palace of tin inside a parlor is an expensive vanity. We are given the mahogany clock and the lace before the iceberg arrives, so that when the sea strikes the grand stair, we may feel the chill without a drop upon our hem. A boy and a maiden hold each other upon a wooden door — there was room enough for two, but the picture insists upon a solitary frost. I watched the great iron chimney go down into the black tea of the Atlantic. It is a curious errand to purchase a shipwreck for an afternoon — and then step out into the quiet dust of the garden. The blue stone thrown into the deep at the end stayed at the bottom, but the ocean in the room was only light. Human pride builds a very tall deck, sir, but the water keeps no ledger of our brass. We like the calamity best when it comes with violins, while the floor tilts like a roof in January. It is the freezing that entertains us, provided the hearth remains warm.

name: Oscar Wilde
essay: Nothing is so completely fatal to the charm of a stroll as the vulgar ambition to measure it. To wander aimlessly is the highest achievement of a refined soul. The moment one begins to count one’s paces, locomotion ceases to be an art and becomes a trade. There is a terrible seriousness in this modern desire to reduce our leisurely rambles to mere arithmetic. Industry has persuaded the public that walking without a tally is a species of idleness, whereas it is, in truth, the only civilised way to spend an afternoon. A gentleman walks to escape his creditors, not to audit his own feet. To turn a promenade into a mathematical exercise is an unpardonable insult to the landscape. It converts a graceful inclination into a tedious duty. One ought to move through the world with supreme indifference to distance. The man who knows precisely how many steps he has taken today has clearly taken far too many. He has substituted the drudgery of the accountant for the joy of the idler. Physical exercise is merely the refuge of those who lack the imagination to remain beautifully still. Besides, any device that rewards one for achieving a numerical quota only encourages the disastrous habit of perseverance.

name: Franz Kafka
essay: The surgeon's assistant, who had been sent to explain to me what I would not be permitted to feel, spoke so quietly and with such regard for the hour that I did not like to interrupt him, though I had already understood the greater part. It was a matter of a mask, he said, and of counting, and he named a number from which I was to begin, a number that seemed to have been chosen not for my sake but for the sake of some earlier patient whom it had suited. I was to count backwards. Whether I would arrive at the end of the counting, he could not say, since nobody had ever been asked afterwards, and the question of asking afterwards belonged, as he put it, to another department. I said that I preferred to remain awake for the cutting, if only to witness that it was being done properly. He nodded, wrote something down, and told me that this wish was entirely reasonable and could not be granted, because the cutting took place in a room I would not be in. The pain, however, would be there, quite undisturbed, waiting in the next room with the instruments, and would be handed back to me later, a little reduced, together with my coat.

name: Oscar Wilde
essay: To be truly civilised is simply a matter of possessing immaculate manners and an extravagant passion for marmalade. Nothing is quite so refreshing as a stranger who arrives in London equipped only with polite enthusiasm and a tag around his neck. The world insists upon treating hospitality as a dreary civic duty, yet here it is elevated to an exquisite art form. We must always admire a guest who wrecks a domestic bathroom with such flawless grace that catastrophe feels like a gesture of high breeding. Manners, after all, are far more vital than morals, and a bright blue duffle coat will cover a multitude of sins. The English have always preferred innocence when it comes dressed in felt and carries citrus conserve. It is dreadfully easy to be cynical, but to remain entirely good-natured without becoming tedious is a magnificent triumph of style. Society will always forgive a stranger who causes utter ruin, provided he does so with supreme courtesy and a hard stare. Realism in art has always been the refuge of the unimaginative. Give us instead the sublime absurdities of polite bears, for they remind us that life is far too important a thing ever to be discussed seriously.

name: Friedrich Nietzsche
essay: I have watched the civilised herd gather in the dark to shiver before the sea. For generations they have laboured to eliminate terror from their lives: they build seawalls, draft ordinances, insure their fragile property against every chance encounter. Still, they cannot endure the flat monotony of their own security. They must pay for the image of a leviathan simply to feel their hearts beat. In that grey, silent water, nature reveals her true character: cold, indifferent, driven solely by hunger. The beast possesses no morality, no malice, no desire for vengeance: it simply consumes. Observe how the inhabitants of the shore meet this primitive force. The mayor worries for his holiday revenue: the scientist categorises the monster: the old hunter treats nature as a personal enemy to be insulted. They demand that the deep be made manageable, reduced to a problem for local governance and iron harpoons. When the creature finally explodes into splinters, the survivors rejoice: they believe they have triumphed over the wild. They return to their shallow beaches, persuaded that the world has been made safe for their leisure. They are mistaken: they have merely bought themselves another summer of self-deception.

name: George Orwell
essay: If you sit in a public house today, you will see young men and women flicking their thumbs across small glass screens, discarding photographs of human faces at the rate of one every two seconds. A face appears, is judged in a fraction of a second, and is brushed aside with a twitch of the finger. It is done with the cold efficiency of a clerk sorting bad apples in a shed. What strikes one about this habit is not that people wish to find a companion, but that they have turned courtship into a form of solitary work. One does not talk to a neighbour over a pint; one inspects fifty strangers in a row and rejects forty-nine of them without ever hearing them speak. The whole business rests on the silly idea that human character can be judged by the shape of a nose or the slant of a hat. In truth, it breeds a shallow, restless temper. When the choice seems endless and costs nothing, no one can remain content with the person sitting opposite them, because there is always another face waiting beneath the thumb. We think we are choosing freely, but we have merely agreed to treat each other as cheap manufactured goods.

name: Jane Austen
essay: Mrs. Harcourt has been listening, she tells me, to a gentleman who speaks for two hours together upon the history of salt, and she assures me she has never passed a more improving week. I could not doubt her, as she had been a full quarter of an hour in the telling of it. The gentleman, it seems, is not in the room, nor in the county, nor, so far as anyone can determine, under any obligation to be correct; but he is heard in the kitchen, the carriage and the shrubbery, and wherever a lady has hands occupied and a mind at liberty, he is received with a cordiality that many a living neighbour has sought in vain. I do not dispute the pleasure of it. Conversation without the inconvenience of reply must appear to most people a very perfect arrangement, and there are houses in which I have sat where it would have been accepted as a kindness to all parties. Two gentlemen who agree in everything, and who are never at a loss for a third subject, may certainly be borne for an afternoon. But I observed that Mrs. Harcourt, who had learnt so much of salt, could not recall what her own daughter had said at breakfast, and was a little surprised to be told that she had said anything.

name: Franz Kafka
essay: The water was hot, and that was the first difficulty, since a warmth so freely given seemed to require some form of acknowledgement, and I could not discover to whom it should be addressed. The pipes ran into the wall behind the tiles, the wall belonged to the house, the house belonged to a man who lived, so I was told, on the other side of the river and who had never been seen by anyone I knew to turn a tap. I stood beneath it with my eyes closed.
