It would have been easy to say that I was washing, but the washing had been finished some minutes before, and what continued, with the same patience and at the same temperature, was something else, a kind of permission I had not asked for and could not decline without appearing ungrateful to the pipes. I reached for the tap. It is only fair to say that it turned. But the turning, which I had imagined as an ending, proved to be a slight alteration of the water's opinion, and for a while it ran on more quietly, as though it had merely been asked to lower its voice. Outside the curtain the towel hung where I had left it, nearly within reach, and I understood that I was nearly finished, which is the only condition in which anyone is ever found.

name: George Orwell
essay: A bear in a duffle coat arriving at a railway station is the sort of nonsense that succeeds only because the people involved treat it as a practical matter. The Browns do not adopt him out of grand sentiment or political duty. They take him home because it is raining, he has a luggage label round his neck, and it would be plain rude to leave him standing by the lost property office. The pleasure of the picture comes from this dry, English insistence on routine. When the bear floods the bathroom or wrecks a staircase, the disaster is treated not as a tragedy, but as an annoying domestic mishap to be cleaned up before tea. What is striking is how much decency survives in these small, everyday habits. The villain, a museum curator who wants to stuff the animal and put him in a glass case, represents that particular modern urge to classify, exploit and display everything for profit. Against this stands nothing more complicated than good manners, a warm bath, and a marmalade sandwich kept under a hat for emergencies. It is a very quiet sort of patriotism, but it is far more convincing than any speech.

name: Leo Tolstoy
essay: Men who do not work with their hands assemble in digital groups to send each other endless messages that express no genuine thought and serve no useful purpose. In these gatherings, dozens of idle people write without stopping, responding to every trifle and filling their hours with continuous, meaningless talk. They convince themselves that this constant exchange brings them together, but it does not bring them together; it only prevents them from ever remaining quiet with their own consciences or seeing the truth of their existence. A man who spends his day reading and sending hundreds of brief, empty remarks to a crowd of acquaintances becomes incapable of serious thought, incapable of silence, and incapable of true love for his neighbour. Meanwhile, the labouring people must plough the fields, bake the bread, and maintain the very physical machinery that enables these idle men to transmit their senseless chatter across distances. Whatever time a man devotes to this friction of trivial words is time stolen from his moral duties. It is a system designed to keep the privileged classes perpetually occupied with nothing, so that they may never realise the injustice of their lives or the futility of their daily existence.

name: Julia Child
object: reclining a seat on a plane
essay: Look behind you before you do it. That is the whole of the method, and I am astonished at how many people skip it. A reclined seat is a lid coming down on a pot, and the person in the seat behind is the pot. If you have not noticed whether there is a laptop open, or a cup of coffee balanced on the tray, or a pair of knees already pressed against the plastic, you have no business pushing the button. I do not say you must never recline. I am not a Puritan, and an inch or two of angle in the small hours of a long flight is a genuine mercy to the spine. But there is a right way. Ease it back slowly, as you would fold egg whites, not slam it down as if the seat had insulted you. Give the person behind a moment to rescue their dinner. Then settle. And I have no patience for the person who reclines fully, immediately after takeoff, in the middle of a meal service. It is bad technique and worse manners. The airline has sold you the lever, certainly, but it has not sold you the other fellow's four inches of breathing room. Use the thing with attention, or leave it alone.

name: Charles Dickens
essay: I met him on the Hungerford stairs at eleven at night, a respectable man of fifty with the collar of a deacon, and he was laughing. He was laughing alone, at nothing, at the river, at the lamp, with his mouth open and his head thrown back, as if the very fog had told him a joke. Two paces on I saw the cause: a small white wire dangled from each of his ears like the roots of some bloodless vegetable, and into that wire two gentlemen, whom he had never met and never would, were pouring an hour and forty minutes of their opinions upon cheese. I do not object to the opinions. I object to the hour and forty minutes. Here are two persons who, in my own day, must have been put to some honest trade, and who now are permitted to prattle without interruption, without correction, without so much as a cough from a bored relation, and to be conveyed in the pocket to every pillow in the kingdom! Nobody stops them. Nobody ever says, Gentlemen, enough. And the listener, poor captive, walks the whole length of London in their company, deaf to the cab, deaf to the beggar, deaf to the plain, unadvertised music of his own thoughts, which have been turned out of doors like a tenant in arrears.

name: George Orwell
essay: If you have a headache after a long morning in a noisy room, you do not rest or go out into the fresh air. You take a white pill from a small cardboard box, swallow it with a glass of tap water, and expect the pain to be gone before lunchtime. It is cheap, clean, and extraordinarily efficient. Yet there is something unhealthy about the ease of it. Pain is the body’s way of saying that you have worked too long, slept too little, or eaten bad food. It is a warning, like a signalman dropping a red flag on the railway line. When you swallow a pill, you are not curing the trouble; you are simply cutting the wire so the alarm stops ringing. This allows a clerk to sit at his desk for another four hours when he ought to be in bed, or a labourer to go on digging a trench with a bad back. We think of it as a mercy, but in practice it is merely a way of keeping the machinery running. A man who can cure his toothache in five minutes will never bother to change his diet, and a society that can abolish discomfort at will soon forgets how to endure it.

name: Hunter S Thompson
essay: The man in the next lane was moving his lips. Not singing, not cursing, just mouthing along to something only he could hear, and when we stalled together at the light on Route 9 I saw the little glowing rectangle on his dashboard and the title scrolling across it, a novel I had once read in a motel in Tucson with a wet towel under the door and a very bad conscience. He was being read to. At sixty miles an hour. By a stranger with a trained voice and a union card. I have no quarrel with the story. My quarrel is with the voice, that smooth professional baritone doing the dialogue of a drunken sheriff as if he were reading the specials at a steakhouse. Prose has a pulse of its own, a bad, crooked, private one, and the narrator has stolen it and sold it back to you at a markup. You no longer hear the book. You hear a man's opinion of the book, delivered in your skull while your hands do something else. And that is the real swindle: the idea that attention can be split like a check. It cannot. Somebody always gets shorted, usually the road. He drove off, still mouthing. I let the light change twice.

name: Virginia Woolf
essay: Consider the cold glass screen standing at the end of the aisle, humming with its pale light. We step up to it with our tins of soup and loaves of bread, forced to play the shopkeeper ourselves. There is a peculiar indignity in waving a packet of butter before an unblinking red beam; the glass remains obstinately dark until the small black stripes are aligned just so. In former days, a girl behind the counter would remark upon the rain, or nod at a parcel of tea, acknowledging that two souls had met across a wooden board. Now, the machine demands our undivided labour, flashing its amber warnings and scolding us in a courteous, metallic chime for placing an unexpected weight upon the shelf. One feels a foolish desire to speak to the aluminium plate, to explain that the lemons were weighed with scrupulous honesty. Beneath this small humiliation, however, lies a quieter exchange. We stand in rows, dutifully scanning our own humble spoils beneath the glare of the electric bulbs, while the shopkeeper observes us from afar, comfortably spared the trouble of our conversation.

name: Marcus Aurelius
essay: Thou wilt be asked to remove thy belt. Remove it. The belt was never thine in any way that matters. Thou wilt stand in a line. A line is only men waiting, and thou art one of them. Thou art no more the exception here than anywhere. The man who looks into thy bag does his work. He did not choose thee. He sees a thousand bags before noon. Give him no cause for contempt, and take none from him. Thou fearest delay. Examine the fear. The hour is not stolen from thee, since it was never promised. Thou hast only the present, and the present is here, between two plastic trays. They ask whether thou carriest anything sharp. Answer plainly. Thou carriest much that is sharp, and none of it is in the bag: the quick word, the sneer at the slow traveller, the claim that thou art owed haste. The machine looks through thy coat and finds nothing. Let it find nothing in thy temper either. They fear what a few men might do. The fear is not foolish, and not thine to mock. Thou also hast guarded a gate against a smaller enemy and called it prudence. Walk through when thou art called. Put on thy shoes. Hold thy tongue.

name: Douglas Adams
essay: The airport lounge works on a principle that would be familiar to anyone who has studied the medieval sale of indulgences: you pay a considerable sum so that you may wait in a better place for the thing you are already waiting for. The thing does not arrive any sooner. It is simply that, while it fails to arrive, you are permitted to sit in a chair that was chosen by someone who had once read about chairs. The lounge is defined chiefly by what it is not, and what it is not is the terminal, which stands a few feet away on the other side of a door that has been fitted with a very serious receptionist. Behind her, everything is the same as outside, only quieter and free, and it is the free that does the work. A person who would not dream of eating a lukewarm sandwich at eleven in the morning will eat three of them, standing up, because they have been included in the price. Nobody in the history of commerce has been so thoroughly persuaded by a sandwich. The real function of the place, I suspect, is to reassure the traveller that the delay is happening to someone of standing. The departures board says the same thing in the lounge as it does everywhere else, but it says it on a better screen, and this is felt, quite sincerely, to be a form of progress.

name: Confucius
essay: The Master said, 'When a man is asked to take off his belt and his shoes before strangers, and does so without complaint, I do not yet know whether he is patient or only tired.' The Master said, 'The officer who looks into my bag may be diligent, or fearful, or merely obedient. The diligent look at the traveller. The fearful look at the bag. The obedient look at the line behind him.' The Master said, 'I have stood a long while in such a line, and my thoughts were not good ones. I counted the faults of the man ahead of me, who had forgotten his coins, and I did not count my own, which were the same.' The Master said, 'A gate that is kept in order is a courtesy of a kind. It says that the road is shared, and that no one has the right to endanger another. But where the gate is kept with suspicion toward all, trust is spent faster than it is earned.' The Master said, 'When the officer says "Please" and means it, the line moves more easily than any machine could move it. When he says it as a rule, it does not.' The Master said, 'I would put up with the shoes. It is the manner of asking that I should wish to see mended, in the one who asks and in the one who answers.'

name: Nora Ephron
essay: The marmalade sandwich under the hat is the thing I keep thinking about. Not the sandwich itself, which is a joke, but the fact that he keeps it there for emergencies, the way my mother kept a twenty-dollar bill folded into the toe of a boot. Paddington is a bear who has been told that London will be kind, and the movie's whole nerve is that it lets him be wrong for about an hour and a half and then makes him right anyway. I went expecting to be charmed and to resent it. I was charmed. I resented nothing. Hugh Bonneville plays the father as a man who has calculated the risk of everything, including breakfast, and I recognized him at once; I have dated him. Nicole Kidman, in her ice-blond bob and her taxidermy kit, is the only villain I have ever wanted to see in a better coat. What the film wants from you is simple. It wants you to say hello to a stranger on the Tube escalator, and it knows you won't, and it forgives you in advance. That's the trick. It is so polite that you leave feeling vaguely accused, and also, I'm sorry to say, hungry. I bought a jar of Dundee marmalade on the way home. It's still in the cupboard. I'm saving it.

name: Marcel Proust
essay: What strikes me, when the face of one of these young women appears on the little lit pane of my telephone, recommending with a radiance of perfectly rehearsed spontaneity a serum, a hotel in the Maldives, a way of folding linen, is not that she is lying, for she is probably sincere, but that her sincerity has been so thoroughly lit from every side, like those portraits by fashionable painters in which the sitter's pearls are rendered with such care that we begin to suspect the sitter herself was added afterwards to give the pearls somewhere to hang, that we can no longer find the spot where the woman ends and the commission begins. I have known, in the salons of my youth, duchesses who made a fashion merely by arriving late in a particular shade of mauve, and their power seemed to me mysterious because it was never confessed; theirs was the authority of a name that had no need to ask. These others ask constantly, and are therefore loved with that peculiar tenderness we reserve for people who flatter us by needing us, so that the multitude, which believes it is following her, is really being counted by her, each admirer a small coin dropped into a purse whose weight she consults between sentences. And yet I cannot quite despise her, since I too once bought a cravat because a man I admired wore one, and wore it, I now suspect, because someone else had.

name: Bertrand Russell
essay: I have been told that a man may now listen to two strangers talk for three hours about a subject on which neither is an authority, and that millions do so willingly. My first impulse was to condemn this. My second was to remember how I have spent a good many evenings, and to hold my tongue. Talk is the oldest of our entertainments, and it was never meant to be edited. The dinner table, the club, the railway carriage supplied it free, and the quality was uneven. What has changed is that the dull remark, once confined to the room in which it was made, can now be preserved and distributed to the whole world. I do not think this has made us wiser; I think it has made us better supplied. Still, there is one real merit. The listener's hands are free, and a man who is washing dishes while hearing an argument about the Roman provinces is better occupied than a man who is washing dishes with nothing in his head but his grievances. Most people's private thoughts are not good company. The danger is that we shall mistake hearing a conversation for taking part in one. Agreeing with a voice in the kitchen costs nothing, and it is worth about that.

name: Henry David Thoreau
essay: I went to see the ogre because I was told he lived in a swamp, and I confess I was prepared to like any man who would. He has the sense to keep a mud-hole of his own, a onion for his supper, and a sign on his fence; he asks of the world only that it stay on the far side of the post. For perhaps ten minutes this is the best economy on the screen. Then the swamp is overrun by eviction notices and fairy-tale refugees, and he must trot off to win it back from a lord who is, I take it, five feet tall and owns a castle. The bargain is this: he is to fetch a princess in exchange for his own quiet. I have known farmers strike worse ones, and for less mud. What I cannot forgive is the manner. Every minute of the picture, perhaps ninety-odd of them, is paid for in jokes about other stories, so that the audience laughs only at what it has already been sold elsewhere. The wolf, the pig, the gingerbread man are brought in like borrowed tools and returned unsharpened. The donkey talks as fast as a clerk paid by the word. Yet when the ogre's breath fogs a window in the morning light, or a dragon's chain swings over a lake of real fire, I was caught entirely, and would have stayed the night. The moral, that the green man is as good as the pink, is sound, and cheap, and costs the makers nothing to say.

name: Julia Child
essay: A dinner party for twelve works because someone decides who sits where. Put the same twelve people in a room with no host, no table and no hour at which to go home, and you have a group chat. I cannot say I admire it. Consider what goes wrong. Everyone speaks at once, nobody waits for the sauce to finish, and a question about Saturday is answered on Tuesday by someone who has plainly not read the first forty messages. The cook in me is appalled. Conversation, like a good stock, wants proportion and a little patience, and here is a pot into which every guest throws whatever is in his pocket. And yet I will not be entirely sour about it. When a sister reports that the roast is out of the oven and the family may come, and nine people answer within a minute, that is a table of a sort. That is useful, and rather lovely. So here is my method. Keep the group small, as you would a sauce with few ingredients. Give it one purpose. Say plainly what you mean, once, and then stop. Mute it when you must, without apology, as you would close the kitchen door on a noisy dog. And for anything that matters, a birthday, a quarrel, a death, telephone, or better, go and sit down together.

name: Sun Tzu
essay: A small face carries a message that a paragraph cannot, and a paragraph carries a message the face cannot. The commander who knows the difference wins the exchange before it begins. If the message is an order, send no face with it. A smile laid upon a command tells the soldier it may be argued. If the message is a reproof, send no face with it either. The yellow grin softens the blow, and the blow was meant to land. If the message is a thanks, send the face. Few words, one sign, and the matter is closed. If a stranger sends you a thumb, read it as a door shut politely. If an ally sends you a row of tears and laughter, read his mood, not his words, for he has stopped choosing among them. There are not many faces in common use, yet the same face means mirth to the young, scorn to the old, and nothing at all to the man who has not looked at it twice. Where a sign has two meanings, the enemy of your meaning is not the rival but the reader. Do not send a doubtful sign to a distant reader. If you wish to learn a man's temper, count his faces. He who sends none is guarded or cold. He who sends many is open, or hiding behind the crowd.

name: Franz Kafka
essay: The little faces arrived on my table in the morning, as they do every morning, without any signature, so that I could not say whether the sender intended the one with the tears of laughter to be read as joy or as the exhaustion that follows a very long joke at the sender's own expense. I answered with the plain yellow face that merely smiles, which I had been told was the safest, and which I then learned, from a cousin who works in the offices of the insurance company and is therefore reliable in such matters, is the one that is understood nowhere as it was meant to be. I tried the folded hands. They were taken, I was informed after some days, as a request, although I had intended them as thanks, and the thanks, being a request, had to be granted or refused by someone whose name was not given to me. In the meantime the sender had added a small flame. I do not say the flame was hostile. I say only that nobody has ever shown me the register in which its meaning is entered, and that I have spent three evenings, with a patience I still consider reasonable, composing a reply made entirely of letters, which is thought to be too severe, and is therefore not yet sent.

name: Jane Austen
essay: There is a particular species of household in which the hour of rising has always been a matter of the most delicate negotiation, and it is to such families that the little bell upon the washstand must be thought a peculiar blessing, or a peculiar affront, according to the temper of the person it addresses. Formerly, a young woman who wished to be early had only her conscience to rely upon, a servant who might or might not be disposed to knock, and the kindness of the sun; and as the first was seldom consulted before ten, the second was generally occupied elsewhere, and the third had no authority in November, her good intentions were commonly overtaken by her breakfast. The new contrivance admits of no such indulgence. It speaks at the appointed minute, without regard to the lateness of the previous evening or the merit of the dream it interrupts, and it speaks again, with rather less patience, a few minutes after. I confess there is something to be respected in a monitor so entirely free of compliment. Yet I observe that those who are most obliged to it are generally the least grateful, and that the hand which silences it in the morning is the same which, in the evening, has taken such pains to set it.

name: George Orwell
essay: A clerk sitting at his desk in a dark woollen coat likes to imagine that his real life is happening somewhere else. The picture houses profit from this belief by telling him that the office he works in, the rain outside, and the cold tea in his cup are all part of a vast lie invented by machine men to keep him quiet. It is a very comforting idea. If the world is merely a trick played upon your senses, you are no longer responsible for your own misery. You do not have to ask why you take orders from a manager you dislike, or why you spend your evenings in a draughty parlour; you can simply pretend that none of it is real. The trouble with this sort of fantasy is that it makes rebellion look too easy. You are invited to believe that by making a single brave choice, by swallowing a small coloured pill in a back room, you can shatter the whole machinery of state power. But real power is never broken by a trick of the mind. It is maintained by policemen, coal miners, and tax collectors, and if you want to change it, you have to do something far more exhausting than watching a man in black spectacles dodge bullets.

name: Marcel Proust
essay: What I had not foreseen, when the machine said in its level, unaccusing voice that there was an unexpected item in the bagging area, was that I should feel myself suspected by no one, and that this absence of a accuser would prove more difficult to bear than any accusation; for a shopkeeper's glance, however unjust, at least confers on the person it falls upon a certain solidity, as the disapproval of a duchess, for those who have never been admitted to her salon, fixes them in a definite place on the social map, whereas here I stood in the condition of a defendant whose judge has been replaced by a scale, and who must therefore plead his innocence to a pan of metal that cannot be moved by tone, by a blush, by the evident honesty of a man holding a single lemon. I lifted the lemon; I set it down; the voice repeated itself without impatience, which was precisely its cruelty, since impatience would have been a human weakness and so a kind of acquaintance. And when at last a young attendant came, passing her card across the screen with the careless authority of a priestess absolving a sin she had not troubled to hear, I understood that I was grateful to her out of all proportion, as one is grateful to the first familiar face on a foreign platform, and that I should have gone on being grateful, had she let me, a half-minute past the lemon.

name: Confucius
essay: The Master said, 'When a man is praised by the whole village, I do not yet know whether he is good. When he is praised by the good in the village and disliked by the bad, then I begin to know.' Of those who are followed by many thousands and are known to none of them, what shall be said? The Master said, 'There are those who are looked at, those who are heard, and those who are trusted. The first is easily had, the second with some labour, the third only after a long time.' Tsze-kung asked whether a man who is much followed must be worthy. The Master said, 'A crowd gathers at a fire for the warmth, and it does not ask who cut the wood.' The Master said, 'The ancient wished to be known, but only after he had made himself worth knowing. Now men show their faces first and hope the worth will come after, as one might set the table before there is any grain.' The Master said, 'I have watched a man speak well of a meal he has not eaten, and I have been that man in small matters. To speak of the way is easy. To walk it where no one is looking is the difficulty.'

name: Anthony Bourdain
essay: The first thing I ever did in a real restaurant kitchen that anybody thanked me for was run the whites. Aprons, side towels, the chef's jackets with the sleeves stiff as cardboard from veal stock and clarified butter. A Speed Queen in the basement, bolted to a floor that was always wet, next to the dry storage and a mop bucket nobody had emptied since the Carter administration. Ninety minutes a load. Miss your window and you'd be wiping a station down with a towel that smelled like a drowned dog. So I have no patience for people who talk about the thing as a convenience. It isn't one. It's a debt you stopped noticing. Somebody used to stand at a river, or a copper, or a washboard, with forearms like rope and knuckles split open by lye, and that somebody was almost always a woman, almost never paid properly, and nobody wrote her name down. Now you thumb a dial, walk away, and feel nothing. I do it too. Every week. Pods, cold cycle, a podcast in my ears. But the laundress is still out there. She works the night shift at a hospital linen plant, in heat that would flatten you, folding what you bled on. Think of her when the buzzer goes.

name: Virginia Woolf
essay: Consider the heavy wool coat, unbuttoned in haste and laid flat in a shallow grey tray. Alongside it goes the small, intimate clutter of our pockets—the brass keys, the folded letter, the pen with its nib safely retracted—exposed under the indifferent glare to strangers who do not know our names; yet we offer them up with a docile, almost rhythmic obedience. We step forward without our boots, feeling instantly diminished in height and absurdly delicate upon the cold floor, as though stripped not merely of leather, but of that protective varnish with which a civilised person moves through a crowd. What do we hope to prove by this awkward surrender? That we harbour no harm, perhaps; but the mind rebels against the cold inspection of the tall frame as we pass through its upright arch. One gathers the warm coat, buckles the belt once more, and slides the silver coins back into the dark of a pocket. The whole spectacle ends as abruptly as it began, leaving behind only the faint, foolish sensation of having stood bare-footed before an unseen judge.

name: Marcus Aurelius
essay: Thou hast a voice in thy ear all day. Ask who is doing the thinking. Another man has read the book. Another man has chosen the pace, the pauses, the weight on each word. Thou hast only to sit still and be carried. This is pleasant. Call it what it is. The hands are busy with the pot or the plough. The mind is told to follow a stranger. Neither task is done with the whole of thee. Thou art in two places and in neither. A book read with the eye lets thee stop. Thou canst return to a sentence and weigh it. The voice moves on whether thou hast weighed it or not. Much passes through thee that never stays. Do not count the hours listened. Count what thou hast changed in thyself because of them. If the number is nothing, the hours were idle, however full they felt. There is a use for it. The road is long and the work is dull, and a good sentence is better company than thy own complaints. Take it then, as thou takest bread. Bread feeds the body only when it is eaten, and a sentence feeds the mind only when it is questioned. Switch it off sometimes. Sit with the silence, and answer thyself.

name: Charles Dickens
essay: I came out of that picture-house with my hat in my hand, and I have no recollection of taking it off. Let the reader who has seen the thing say whether he, too, did not walk home along the dry middle of the road, at a respectful distance from every gutter, kerb, and puddle in the parish. What I resent, and shall go on resenting until I am in my grave, is the shabby cunning of it. For the better part of an hour the monster is not shown at all. We are given a yellow barrel bobbing upon the water; we are given a pair of legs kicking in the green dusk, as helpless as a pair of tongs; we are given two notes of music, only two, repeated like a clerk's cough in a counting-house, and by these we are driven like sheep. Is it honest to frighten a man with a cello? Is it fair to tickle the dread out of him with a fiddle-string, and then, when he is quite undone, to present him with a rubber fish the length of a omnibus? And yet I confess it did its work, and I screamed, sir, I screamed. The true villains, to my eye, are the Corporation gentlemen, who keep the bathing open for the sake of the summer trade, and will count the bodies later. Their ledger-minded cowardice frightened me more than any teeth.

name: David Foster Wallace
essay: Last Tuesday my sister texted me that our aunt's biopsy was benign, and then, after the sentence, the little yellow face with the single tear and the smile, the one that is supposed to mean relieved-but-also-moved, and I felt the relief arrive about a full second after I felt something else, which was a kind of clerical gratitude that she had picked the right one. There are, I looked it up, something over three thousand to choose from. She picked the tear-and-smile. Not the grimace, not the folded hands, not the face with the little sweat drop that means, as far as I can tell, a nervousness so mild it has to be apologized for. I want to say this is a language, and I want to say it is not, and I notice that which one I say depends mostly on whether I am the sender or the receiver. Sending, I am a poet. Receiving, a forensic accountant. Did the thumbs-up from my editor mean approval or merely that the message had been processed? I spent eleven minutes on it. That is the thing. The face is supposed to save effort, and instead I am parsing a cartoon like a clause in a lease, which says less about the cartoon than about me, a grown man who cannot bear to be unambiguous and cannot bear to be ambiguous on purpose either.

name: Franz Kafka
essay: The message had been sent at a quarter past nine, and since then, so far as B. could tell from the small grey figures beneath it, it had been read by eleven of the fourteen members, among them two who had said at the beginning, in the only message they had ever written there, that they would probably leave soon. B. had meant to answer that evening. He had merely wished to say that the Thursday date was acceptable to him, provided it was not the Thursday already mentioned by someone whose name he did not recognise and who had since written nothing, though it was clear from the thumbs raised beneath that person's remark that the remark had been taken as settled. To reply now would be to reply to the whole group, which was not what he intended, for the question concerned only the man who had asked it, and that man, as B. discovered when he looked more closely, was not among the fourteen at all, having been added and removed in the same minute. To write to him separately was possible. It would, however, be noticed in the larger group that B. had stopped writing there, and the silence would be counted against him, as every silence was, though no one had ever said so. He put the telephone face down and turned it over again almost at once, because it had trembled.

name: Emily Dickinson
essay: Green light running down black glass is a shallow embroidery. A person might sit in a parlor and mistake the stitches for the World—until the needle strikes the bone. I tried the little scarlet morsel—it tasted of iron and well water. It is an unkindness to unthread a mind from its own sleep, yet once the knot is cut, the linen cannot be re-sewn. They show us a glass jar where the Soul was kept warm, fed on a syrup of days to keep the tenant quiet. I prefer my own frost, though it bite the heel. The tall Gentleman with the dark spectacles offers a choice between a comfortable slumber and a cold hearth. To choose the hearth is to discover that the sky was only painted paper, stretched over iron ribs. They bend a silver spoon to prove the Air is supple—yet the spoon is useless if it will not hold the soup. To tell a Man his life was merely a dream borrowed from a Machine is a bitter medicine. Yet having seen the seam, who could wear the garment again? I set the world down upon the table. It was far too light to hold a soul.

name: Friedrich Nietzsche
essay: I distrust this modern eagerness to exchange a human gaze for a lighted monitor: it is the clearest confession of a spirit too feeble to endure the mildest friction of an encounter. The buyer stands before the glass arbiter and calls his submission efficiency—he misinterprets his own cowardice as a triumph of reason. To look another man in the eye during the small transactions of life requires a fragment of force, a minimal exercise of willpower; to obey an automated prompt requires only the passivity of a trained beast. Modern man has grown so soft, so thoroughly unsettled by the living presence of his neighbour, that he constructs a silent overseer to handle his daily bread. He accepts the machine's red scolding without a protest—the individual who demands supreme deference from his equals submits without a murmur to a glowing chime. Convenience is the altar upon which he sacrifices the last remnants of his fortitude. He fancies himself a master commanding an obedient tool: he is a coward constructing a sanctuary where no human eye can ever reach him.

name: Michel de Montaigne
essay: I confess that I have sat in one of these rooms for three hours with a plate of small cheeses before me, not hungry, and been nearly content; and the contentment troubled me more than any discomfort would have done. I had paid, or my card had paid, for the privilege of waiting apart from those who wait without it, and I looked through the glass at the crowd by the gates with a feeling I should be ashamed to name aloud, though I will name it here: it was the pleasure of not being them. Is this so very different from the habit of the noble who stood nearer the king at table, and was thought the taller for the standing? I suspect not. Yet I would not wholly condemn the room. A man who has been shoved about, announced at, and searched to his stockings may be forgiven for wanting a chair that does not face a loudspeaker; and I notice that my temper, which is poor, improves on soft leather, which says little for my philosophy. What I cannot settle is whether the quiet there is rest or only the absence of noise, as a man who has left off beating his servant is not therefore gentle. The others around me stared at small lit screens, and I at them, and none of us, I think, were anywhere; we had been set down in a pleasant nowhere between two places, and I am not sure I did not prefer it to both.

name: George Orwell
essay: Heavy wet linen is one of the most stubborn things in the world. Anyone who has ever had to scrub a cotton shirt over a tin board until his knuckles bleed knows that washing clothes by hand is not a light chore, but hard physical labour. The box in the corner, which sloshes water through dirty coats at the turn of a switch, has done more to lighten the daily work of the home than almost any other gadget. It does not merely save time; it saves muscle and skin. A woman who spent her Mondays bent over a steaming tub, smelling of soda and damp wool, now drops her washing into a metal drum and goes about her business. Yet there is a small penalty attached to this comfort. Because the machine makes washing effortless, we demand that our clothes be washed ten times more often than our grandfathers thought necessary. A garment worn for a few hours is thrown into the tub simply because it is no longer fresh. The drudgery has gone, but the standard has risen to meet the machine's capacity, so that the tub spins almost every day.

name: Walt Whitman
essay: Four-thirty, February, the room black and the window glazed with frost; and then the thing goes off on the shelf beside the bed. Brass bell, hammer, spring, a tin case with a dial that glows a little green. I have heard it in the boarding-house walls, through the floor from the clerk below, down the whole row of back bedrooms--one after another, like pistols down a line. Then the boots on the boards, the pitcher and basin, the cold water, the stove-door, the coffee-pot, the lunch-pail pick'd up off the table. I confess I like it. Not the sound, which is a rasp, a insult to a sleeper; but what the sound sets going. The ferryman gets to the slip, the baker to his ovens, the printer to his case and type, the car-driver to the horses, the washerwoman to her tubs--all of them rous'd by the same little wound-up engine, bought for a dollar or less, and no king's chamberlain required. Once the cock did it, and the sexton's rope, and the neighbor's knuckle on the shutter. Now each man keeps his own watchman under his own roof. He is a tyrant, true; I have cursed him. Yet I would not send him away.

name: Charles Dickens
essay: I was kept waiting, one wet forenoon, upon the threshold of a certain shipping company, by a small oblong window in the corner of a screen, which informed me that Clarissa was typing. Clarissa was not typing. Clarissa had never possessed a finger, a thumb, a corn, or a chilblain; yet three little dots rose and fell beneath her name, like the breathing of a gentleman feigning sleep in a railway carriage, for the sole purpose of persuading me that a Person was labouring on my behalf. I object to the dots. I object to them as I would object to a butler painted upon the front door, with a painted candle, and a painted bow. Let the machine answer me, if it must; it answers fluently, tirelessly, with the bland and boundless courtesy of a hotel-keeper who has never once been obliged to pay the baker. But let it not sit down at my table in the borrowed coat of a human hesitation. And what, pray, is the end of my question? Why, I am thanked for my patience, assured of my importance, and handed back, with a flourish, to the very spot from which I set out. Sixty minutes, sir; sixty minutes of apology, and not one grain of remedy. The Circumlocution Office has learned to type, and has acquired a pleasing manner.

name: Friedrich Nietzsche
essay: I have watched this small, dripping wanderer conquer the English drawing room: it is a triumph of domestic deceit. What the modern herd adores in this bear is not nature, but nature thoroughly disarmed, sweetened, and taught to tip its hat. They wish to believe that the stranger at the gate brings no terror, no wildness, no instinct: only an appetite for marmalade and a lesson in polite forbearance. How comforting for them! It is the supreme fantasy of a decadent culture: that the untamed wilderness will gladly bow before tea and good manners. They laugh when he floods the bath; they shudder when a villain threatens his skin; yet what they truly celebrate in the theatre is their own safety, their own immunity from primitive impulse. Real force has been banished; the beast is reduced to a helpless orphan; and the civilised family adopts him precisely because his weakness poses no threat to their comfortable routine. This is the morality of the hearth elevated to a grand ideal: to be harmless is to be good, and to be fragile is to be noble. It is a damning confession: the modern soul can tolerate existence only when it is rendered small, soft, and completely manageable.

name: Jane Austen
essay: My brother Henry's acquaintance in the medical line informs me that a gentleman of his profession is accounted skilful in proportion to his despatch, and that the surgeon who can remove a limb in the time it takes a family to rise from table is thought to have shown the greater tenderness. The patient is held, the room is cleared of such ladies as might be overcome, and the whole affair is concluded with so much regularity that those who attend it are generally agreed it was borne remarkably well. I have known a lady praised for her fortitude on an occasion when she had no choice in the matter, and a gentleman for his composure when he had been strapped to a chair. It is natural to wish that so much courage were less often required, and I confess that were any preparation known by which a person might be spared the sensation, while the operation proceeded as usual, I should think it the most agreeable discovery of the age. One can hardly suppose it would be refused. The patient would be relieved; the surgeon, no longer obliged to be quick, might be permitted to be careful; and the friends in the next room would be at liberty to attend to their tea instead of listening for the end of it, though I do not doubt some of them would feel the want of occupation.

name: Walt Whitman
essay: Saw it at last, in a dark hall full of people, and came out into the daylight a little ashamed of how I had gripped the arm of the seat. Beach, umbrellas, pails, a dog, a boy on a yellow raft, the chief with his chum-ladle and his eyes on the water; that is the stuff of it, and the picture knows the worth of such stuff. The fish itself is kept back a long while. What you get is the surface, the fin, the barrels, the cable going taut, a man's face turning--and the dread comes of what is not shown. I call that honest craft; a showman who understands the crowd, and the crowd's appetite to be frighten'd together. The three men in the boat please me best. The sheriff afraid of water, the young scientist with his instruments and his money, the old fisherman with his scraping nail and his Indianapolis story told low in the cabin, scars compared, songs, whiskey, the night before the work. Here is the real thing, men of different callings made equal by an enemy. Then the boat breaking up under them, plank by plank, engines, rail, galley; the tools of the trade turn'd against the tradesman. It wants us to shudder, and we do. It wants us also to stand by one another, and that part I believe.

name: Emily Dickinson
essay: A paper volume waits upon the desk until requested — it yields its quiet ink only when the eye goes seeking. This spoken page arrives by another path. It enters the apron pocket and talks while the dough is kneaded, offering a reader whose lungs I did not borrow. The assistance is curious. When the printed line strikes too sharp, the thumb may shut the cover and hold the solitude fast; the spoken sentence keeps its pace, striding across the kitchen whether the listener is ready or no. It leaves the hands free for the dish and the duster, yet it occupies the ear with an unasked tenant. I listened while folding the morning's wash. The narrative advanced without a pause, but the linen was folded crooked — two intentions cannot inhabit one wrist. It is a modern thrift to buy a story that reads itself, yet it takes from the room that sacred delay where a thought might settle. A voice in the dark is a candle brought by a stranger. It lights the passage, but it chooses where the shadow falls.

name: Marcus Aurelius
essay: Thou standest under the water until the body is warm. Then thou wishest to stay. This wish is not thine. It belongs to the skin. The heat asks for nothing. It gives, and thou takest. Mark how quickly the taking becomes a claim. Yesterday it was a pleasure. Today thou art owed it. The body is a poor master. It wants warmth and it wants more warmth. Give it what is needed. Give it no more. Water was once fetched. It was carried and heated over a fire, and a man knew its price. Thou knowest no price now. Whatever costs thee nothing thou wilt waste. There is a morning duty waiting beyond the door. It does not care whether the water was hot. It asks only whether thou art awake. Observe how the mind loosens here. Thoughts come easily in the steam. Some of them are good. Write those down and leave the rest to the drain. The cold tap is within reach. Turn to it sometimes. Let the body learn that it can bear what it fears. A man who cannot rise from warm water is not free. Rise when the work calls. Dry thyself and go out to it.

name: Henry David Thoreau
essay: I asked the machine last evening how long it takes a pond to freeze, and it answered in four seconds, in nine hundred words, with a courtesy I have never received from a neighbor. I confess I was pleased. It is something to be answered at all. But the pond lies a mile and a quarter from my door, and I have known it to take a man eleven winter mornings of lying on his belly on the black ice, with his cheek to the cold and his breath fogging the glass, to learn what those nine hundred words only repeat. The words were correct. They were also, I think, nobody's. Observe the economy of it. A farmer's boy will carry a pail of water a quarter mile for a penny and know to the cupful what he has carried. This engine carries a whole well to you for nothing, and you drink without once feeling the handle in your palm. What is got for nothing is commonly paid for in some other coin; here, I suspect, in the habit of asking, which grows while the habit of looking shrinks, like a muscle in a sling. Still, when it hesitated, and said it could not be certain, I heard in that confession something nearer honesty than most sermons offer. Let it say so oftener, and let me go see the ice.

name: Virginia Woolf
essay: A silver clip upon the waistband, or a dark band upon the wrist, sits measuring our progress through the London dusk. We set out to watch the light settle over the park, to see the lamps lit along the Embankment, yet our ankles now move under a quiet surveillance. How strange that a walk, once the most lawless of our domestic liberties, should be reduced to arithmetic. We used to measure a stroll by the quality of leaves falling or the turn of a neighbour's voice; now a silent tally ticks against the ribs, demanding its daily toll before the night is declared well spent. It transforms the aimless wanderer into an accountant of her own boots. Yet if we glance down at the small screen glowing in the shadows, there is a curious solace in its quiet precision. The mind may drift into melancholy, unanchored and chaotic; the little machine insists that five thousand paces have indeed occurred, that ground was struck, that the solid earth held firm. We stop by the park railings, touch the cold glass on the wrist, and watch a red bus rumble past through the fog.

name: Julia Child
essay: Somebody will tell you that listening to a book is not reading it, and somebody else will tell you it is exactly the same, and both of them are wrong in ways worth looking at. I came to it by way of the sink. A great heap of dishes, a pot with something burnt onto the bottom, and a voice in the room reading me a novel: the dishes went faster, and I scarcely noticed the scrubbing. That is a real gift, and I am entirely for it. Drudgery is not improved by being silent. But mind what you are doing. A page lets you stop, go back, and look again at the sentence that puzzled you; a voice marches on whether you are ready or not. And the reader matters enormously! A good one is like a good butcher, who gives you the thing cut properly and then gets out of the way. A bad one, all swooping and sighing and performing every character, is the cook who cannot leave the sauce alone, and he will ruin the book for you quite as surely. So choose your reader as carefully as your knife. Use the book for the dishes, the driving, the long walk. For anything that needs real thought, sit down, open it, and pay attention.

name: Friedrich Nietzsche
object: reclining a seat on a plane
essay: I distrust the creature who requires a mechanical button to alter his stance toward existence. Consider the ease with which space is stolen: a traveller depresses a hidden latch, leans his body backward, and imagines he has conquered his discomfort. He has done nothing of the kind. He has merely transferred his fatigue onto the knees of his neighbour, executing this intrusion without the courage of eye contact. Here is malice without risk—a quiet, automated encroachment upon another man's territory. The sufferer demands relief from the strain of sitting upright, which is the proper, disciplined burden of consciousness: he refuses to claim space openly. Instead, he hires a hidden spring to commit his offence for him. He closes his eyes in blissful ignorance, treating the reduced space of the man behind him as a law of nature rather than the direct consequence of his own flaccid will. Sitting upright demands force, tension, a pride in one's posture: reclining is a surrender to gravity, a confession of exhaustion disguised as a right. The mechanism does not serve human dignity: it merely organises human cowardice.

name: Franz Kafka
essay: For some weeks I had meant to withdraw my name, and on the evening I finally sat down to do it I found that the page offering this was reached only through a page about my career, which in turn could be entered only after I had confirmed that the career in question was mine. I confirmed it. A small notice thanked me for my commitment and asked whether I wished to tell them why I was leaving, and since the question seemed to be part of the procedure and not an invitation, I chose from the reasons provided the one that was least untrue, namely that I had received too many messages. The next morning there were eleven more. Three congratulated me on a position I had not taken up, though I could not rule out that it had been taken up on my behalf, and one, from a man whose name I did not know, hoped that I was well and wished to add me to his network, which he described as modest. I did not answer, having learned that an answer is entered somewhere and read by someone, while silence is entered as well, only less carefully. My request, I was told, was being processed. It remains so. In the meantime I am endorsed, each week, for a skill I have never claimed.

name: Benjamin Franklin
essay: I have seen a man's leg taken off above the knee, and I confess the operation was the lesser part of the horror; the greater was the waiting, the straps, and the surgeon's boast that he finish'd in under a minute, as if the patient were to be grateful for the speed of his torment. Speed was then the whole of the art, there being no other mercy to be had; a surgeon was valued by his quickness and his strong assistants, and not at all by his tenderness. If it be true that a vapour can now be breath'd which takes away the sense of the knife, and that the sufferer wakes without remembering it, I count this among the few discoveries that are worth more than they cost, and the cost, I understand, is small. I will own it has a use beyond the patient's ease. A surgeon who need not hurry may take care; he may search for the cause, and not merely cut at the symptom; and many an operation judg'd too cruel to attempt must now be reckon'd possible. Whether men will be wiser for it I doubt, since they commonly spend a new liberty as fast as they receive it. But a mercy is not to be refus'd because it may be abus'd; and I would rather be a fool who felt nothing than a philosopher who felt everything.

name: Jane Austen
essay: A family of my acquaintance, consisting of three sisters, a brother, and a mother who is thought to be above the weaknesses of her children, have lately established among themselves a perpetual conversation, to which each is summoned at every hour by the little instrument she carries, and from which none can decently withdraw without being supposed to have taken offence. It is a most convenient arrangement for the dissemination of intelligence. Whatever the eldest has heard at breakfast is known to the youngest before the tea is cold, and an engagement may be proposed, debated, abandoned, and proposed again, without any one of the party having been obliged to leave her chair, or to look at another. The mother, I am told, replies to everything, and generally to the wrong remark. The brother replies to nothing, but is understood to be gratified by all. The second sister, who has an opinion of her own wit, writes a great deal in the evening, and is rewarded by a small mark of approval from whoever happens to be passing. Nobody quarrels, for to quarrel would require an audience of fewer than five; and so a coolness, when it comes, is conducted by silence, and discovered only by the company's remarking how very quiet the morning has been.

name: George Orwell
essay: A man sitting down to write a letter of thanks or an apology is forced, for a few minutes, to think about what he actually means. He has to weigh one word against another, reject the phrase that sounds false, and stick to what is true. When he hands that job over to a machine, he is not merely saving his time; he is avoiding the unpleasant business of having a mind of his own. The machine will produce three paragraphs of smooth, civilised English in two seconds. It will say all the right things in the standard manner, without a single mistake in grammar or a single drop of real conviction. Ask it to write a letter to a landlord or a speech for a wedding, and it turns out the same neat, grey prose every time. It never hesitates, it never gets angry, and it never says anything that could offend a town clerk. The danger is not that the machine talks like a man, but that men will soon choose to talk like the machine. Once you get used to letting a mechanical voice speak for you, your own thoughts grow lazy. It is simpler to accept the borrowed phrase than to forge your own, and before long you lose the habit of independent thought.

name: Marcel Proust
essay: What first struck me, in the swamp where the ogre bathes in mud and polishes his teeth with a slug, was not the vulgarity, which one expects, but the extraordinary care with which the mud had been rendered, so that the film, having announced that it despised the fairy tale, immediately lavished upon a puddle the tenderness that the old illustrators kept for a princess's hair. And I understood that the whole enterprise rests upon this quarrel conducted in the manner of a lover: as a woman who loudly mocks the provincial society in which she was brought up will nevertheless, at the first indiscretion, reproduce its intonations, its little cadences of the voice, so Shrek mocks the book of tales while borrowing from it every tower, every dragon, every tiresome pledge of a kiss. The animated faces, whose skin has that faintly waxen translucence of a hand held before a candle, never quite persuade me of flesh, and Fiona's, in her moment of ordinary happiness, is more disquieting than any of the monsters. Yet the film asks of us only a kind of complicity, the pleasure of being let into a joke already half known to us, and it grants in return a modest consolation: that the ugly may be loved without being altered, a doctrine it proclaims at the very instant it quietly, and rather cravenly, ceases to apply it.

name: Marcus Aurelius
essay: Thou art sitting in a quiet room with a free drink. Thou hast been told this is a reward. What hast thou done to earn it? Thou hast paid. Nothing more. The chairs are softer here than at the gate. The crowd is thinner. Mark this, and mark also what thou dost feel about the crowd. Thou dost feel thyself above it. That feeling is false. The same flight carries thee and them. The same hour of arrival waits for all. A door and a card have not made thee different. Thou wilt eat more than thou needest. The food is free, and the hunger is not real. Eat what the body asks for. Leave the rest. Thou wilt look at the screen again and again. The flight will leave when it leaves. Looking changes nothing. Thou wilt watch the man who is let in behind thee. Thou wilt think he has not the right. That thought is not thy business. A man needs rest. Take it plainly, as a man takes water. Do not call it a distinction. When the call comes, rise at once. Leave the cushion without regret. Thou hast somewhere to be, and the room was never it. Go to the gate.

name: Mark Twain
essay: I went to this picture expecting to be sold a bear, and I was sold one, but the bargain was a good deal better than the goods advertised. The bear is polite. That is the whole of his equipment, and the film has the nerve to build an entire London on it. Everybody else in the town is rude in the ordinary, comfortable way, and he is polite in the way of a creature who was told once, by an aunt, that it would be needed, and has gone on believing her. I found this a more reckless piece of philosophy than most sermons I have sat through, and a good deal more likely to be tried. The villain is a lady who stuffs animals, which I take to be the film's opinion of people who admire a thing chiefly when it holds still. The family are Londoners of the nervous kind, who keep a risk assessment the way other households keep a cat. They are cured, and the cure is a marmalade sandwich kept under a hat. The picture asks only that you be a little kinder for ninety minutes. I was, and I resent how easy it was. I came out and held a door for a stranger, who did not thank me, and I found I did not mind. The bear would have understood.

name: Emily Dickinson
essay: A stain is a faithful record; it remembers where the hem strayed and what the tea spilled. We used to wring such memories out with boiled water and sore knuckles, paying for clean linen with a day’s breath—a stiff penance for Tuesday. Now the tub accepts the dirty dress without a sermon. It shuts its iron door upon our small corruptions and begins its private storm. One hears the water slap against the dark—a tempest caught in a cupboard. It turns grease to froth and soil to nothing, indifferent to the knee that made the dirt. Purity was once a heavy coat, woven from long hours of steam and aching thumbs. This churn makes white a trivial errand. It strips the day’s journey from the collar, leaving only damp wool that has forgotten where it walked. I handle the wet sleeve when the storm subsides; it is cold and innocent, like a slate wiped before the scholar arrives. We have bought a swift absolution from an engine, but the heart retains its spot—it cannot be rinsed in a tub.

name: Anthony Bourdain
essay: Somebody in Nairobi read the worst thing you can imagine so that you wouldn't have to. Nine hours a shift, a cheap headset, a queue of flagged text that included things I won't type here, for a couple of dollars an hour. That's the line cook of this business. Not the engineer with the fleece vest and the funding round. The reader. The labeler. The person who taught the polite machine what not to say by marking, over and over, what was unspeakable. And I use it. Let me be clear about that. I've asked it to fix a paragraph at one in the morning, felt the small, dirty relief of a clean answer arriving instantly, and closed the window like a man leaving a massage parlor. Complicit. Fully. What bothers me is the tone. That unflappable, apologetic, endlessly available courtesy. Nobody is that nice. Nobody in any kitchen I ever worked in was that agreeable at hour eleven. Real help has friction in it, a bad mood, an opinion, a person who might say no, this is garbage, start over. This thing flatters you in a perfect customer-service voice, and you will mistake it for company. Use it. Fine. But know who paid for the manners.

name: David Foster Wallace
essay: Last Tuesday I spent forty-one minutes of a fifty-minute drive to Bloomington listening to two men I have never met discuss a third man I have also never met, and I can report that I retained nothing, and that I was happy. This needs examining. The two men were named, I think, Kyle and Dan, or possibly Kyle and Ben. Kyle laughed before Dan finished his jokes, a courtesy that in a room would be a kind of love and on a recording is a kind of weather. By minute twenty I had begun answering them. Not aloud. Well, once aloud, at a Toyota. Here is what I believe is going on, and I hold the belief loosely, since the person holding it is the same one who nodded at a Toyota. The thing is built so that nobody has to be looked at. Conversation without the labor of a face. You get the warm sound of being included, the cadence of people who have time, and you owe nothing: no follow-up question, no arranged expression, no remembering the dog's name. It is company with the invoice removed. Which would be fine, wonderful even, if I were not also the man who told his sister he was too busy to call. Dan, or Ben, is at least on a schedule. He turns up Thursdays.

name: Franz Kafka
essay: The drum had stopped turning some while before I understood that I was not permitted to open it. The door, which a quarter of an hour earlier had been merely closed, was now locked, and a small lamp beside it, which I took to be a form of explanation, showed a symbol I had not seen on any previous occasion and which resembled, if anything, a key that had been crossed out by someone in a hurry. I stood in the passage with the basket against my hip, since to set it down would have meant admitting that the matter might take longer, and I had no wish to admit this to the machine, still less to the neighbour, whose own washing, I now noticed, hung already on the line in the courtyard, dry, as it had been, I think, every Tuesday. I do not complain of the water, which was drawn in and let out with great regularity, nor of the sound, which at least had the decency to vary. What I could not determine was whether the lock released itself at the end of the programme or only at the end of a further interval that belonged to no programme and was not shown. The booklet I consulted gave several numbers to telephone, all of them for faults I did not have. After a time the lamp went out, and I took this to be the first step, and waited for the second.

name: Joan Didion
essay: My neighbor in the next apartment runs one while she cooks. I know this because the wall is thin and because I have come to know the voices, two men and sometimes a third, who laugh at the same places every evening around seven. They laugh at a quarter past. They laugh again at twenty-five minutes past. She does not laugh. I hear the knife on the board, the water running, the men. The episodes are numbered. This was episode 212, or it was 213. A woman I knew in New York said she listened to one on the way to her mother's house, three hours on the Thruway, and that by Albany she felt she had been told something, though she could not say what. She said the host had a very nice voice. She said it twice. The voice is the thing. It arrives without a face, in a kitchen or a car or at four in the morning in a room with the shades down, and it says we, and it says let's get into it. Nobody has asked to get into anything. Still the dishes are done by the end, the Thruway is behind you, and the men are saying goodnight, goodnight, see you next week, and the wall goes quiet, and I find that I am waiting.

name: Confucius
essay: The Master said, 'I have watched the great ship go down, and I wept, and afterwards I asked myself what had moved me. It was not the water. The water was made by skilful hands, and I knew it.' The Master said, 'The young man and the young woman are poor in years and rich in feeling. The film asks us to love them, and it does not ask gently. Every glance is placed where we must see it; every parting is stretched until the heart gives way. To be led thus is pleasant. To be led thus without noticing is another matter.' The Master said, 'The rich man's betrothed is made stiff and mean, so that the girl may be thought right to leave him. Here the maker saves himself the labour of judging. Where the good are wholly good and the unworthy wholly cold, there is little for the viewer to weigh.' The Master said, 'Yet I did not find the old woman's remembering a small thing. The many who sank are named by nothing but their sleeping in their beds, and the musicians who played on were not asked to speak. The wise would see in them the real measure, the virtuous would be silent before them, and the bold would ask whether they themselves would have stayed. I am not sure that I should.'

name: Virginia Woolf
essay: A slice of buttered toast, two pale figs, and a silver spoon sit upon a linen cloth, arranged not to satisfy an appetite, but to catch the morning light. A young woman tilts her face toward an invisible audience, holding her teacup at a precise angle before she takes a sip. We are accustomed to actors upon a stage, where greasepaint and footlights mark a clear boundary between illusion and the street; here, the domestic room itself has become the theatre, and every private gesture is polished into a shining commodity. She offers us her favourite cream, her morning thoughts, the very texture of her bedsheets, with the generous intimacy of a neighbour. Yet this warmth is a rigorous labour. To live inside such a spectacle is to turn one’s own existence into an ongoing exhibition, where even weariness must find a flattering frame. We gaze through the glass at this lit parlour, amused and perhaps envious of such tidy order. But as she smiles into the glass, one asks what remains of a person when the lamp is extinguished. It is the unrecorded shadow, surely, that keeps the mind whole.

name: Emily Dickinson
essay: A warm rain lives in brass — until a turn of the wrist commands it down. One stands inside a private summer. The cloud is missing, yet the deluge falls, steaming as if the sun had boiled the sky before yielding it to the floor. Rain was ever a sovereign thing, visiting the roof when it pleased and leaving the clover to dry at its own leisure. Here, a bolt of pewter brings sudden August to the shoulders, though December waits outside the latch with white knives. It is a strange mercy to borrow heat from unseen fires, to let a steady torrent wash away the numbness of a winter morning before the kettle has thought to sing. The skin drinks this sudden noon, amazed that weather can be summoned by a turn of silver. Yet when the knob is shut, the tropical sky vanishes without a whisper. The chill returns, sharper for the brief paradise it displaced. We step out trembling — having worn August for five minutes — to find our own small flesh still subject to the frost.

name: Julia Child
essay: I received a letter once that ended with a small yellow face, winking, and I will tell you plainly that I did not know whether I was being thanked or teased. That is the whole trouble. A wink in a room is a wink; you see the eye, the hand on the spoon, the quarter-inch of a smile, and you know exactly what is meant. A little drawing of a wink, dropped at the end of a sentence, is a pinch of something with no label on the jar. Now I am not against it entirely. A quick heart or a thumb is perfectly useful when you are saying only that the soup arrived and it was good. It saves you a line, and I have no patience with the idea that every message must be a composition. But watch what happens when people lean on it. They stop choosing the word. They stop asking what, precisely, they felt, and they hand over a row of tiny pictures and call it expression. It is the cook who reaches for the bouillon cube every single night and wonders why everything tastes alike. So use it as you would salt: lightly, and on purpose. And if you have something truly tender or truly sharp to say, write the sentence! It takes a minute, and it will be remembered.

name: Emily Dickinson
essay: To pin one's name upon a gate, and solicit the passerby for a penny of esteem, is an errand I had thought left to the hawker. Yet here is a parlor where every guest arrives bearing a slate of his own virtues, freshly chalked and offered for inspection. A neighbor shows his ledger of industrious mornings, and another counters with a certificate of diligence—as if the soul were an apprentice to be hired by the hour. I tried on such esteem once—it fitted like a coat of iron, heavy at the hem and cold to the collar. It is a curious thrift that buys acquaintance with testimonials. One collects gentlemen as another collects pewter spoons, counting the row to see if he is wealthy in eyes. They speak of prospects as if the Future were a mill to be driven by their own small wheel. But a name exposed too long in the sun turns yellow, like linen left upon the grass past dusk. I prefer my own small dark, where nobody asks my occupation—and the cricket gives no reference.

name: Charles Dickens
essay: I paid, last Tuesday, the sum of eleven shillings, or its modern cousin, to be locked in a cellar by a young man in a waistcoat; and I paid it, mark me, willingly, and shook his hand upon the threshold, as a gentleman might thank the hangman for the quality of his rope. The cellar was dressed as the study of a vanished Professor. Why the Professor had vanished, and why he had left his affairs in such a condition, nobody thought to inquire. His desk was furnished with a padlock of four wheels, a globe that opened at the equator, and a Bible with a hollow in it, in which the Almighty's pages had been scooped away to lodge a brass key. I confess this last touched me. Let the Professor vanish; let him not vandalise Scripture. My companions were five citizens of the most respectable stamp: a surveyor, two sisters, a person in insurance, and a boy of fourteen who did all the thinking. These worthies fell upon the furniture like bailiffs upon a bankrupt, tearing out drawers, holding candlesticks to the light, and addressing a stuffed owl in terms of passionate entreaty. Sixty minutes, said a clock upon the wall, in red figures, and every minute of the sixty it reproached us. We escaped with four seconds to spare. And from what? From a door that had been bolted on the outside by the very man who then received our gratitude, and our eleven shillings.

name: Michel de Montaigne
essay: I took off my belt this morning, then my shoes, then, with some reluctance, the small knife I use for apples, and I stood in my stockings with my arms raised like a man surrendering to an enemy who has not yet declared himself. I confess I felt no anger; what I felt was nearer to shame, and I have been turning over since whether the shame was for me, or for the officer, or for the whole contrivance. He was civil enough, and tired, and I suspect he believed in it no more and no less than I did; yet we both performed our parts with great gravity, as men do at a funeral for a stranger. I cannot tell whether it keeps anyone safe. I am not competent to say, and I notice that those who speak most firmly on the matter are commonly those who have least looked into it. A danger that never arrives proves either that the watch was good or that it was never needed, and no man can distinguish the two; so the watch grows, and is praised for the very silence it may have had nothing to do with. Still, I wonder whether I do not take some comfort from being searched. There is a peculiar ease in being treated as equally suspect with my neighbour: the bishop loses his shoes beside the pedlar. And if fear must be managed, I know not that a gentler remedy has been found than to give it a ritual, and a queue.

name: George Orwell
object: reclining a seat on a plane
essay: You sit down in an aeroplane and, before the engines have properly warmed, the man in front of you drops his seat back three inches into your knees. He does not turn round to look at you; he simply presses a small plastic button and lets his weight do the rest. The arrangement is designed to make a man feel that he has gained something for himself, when in fact he has merely taken it from his neighbour. If everyone reclines at once, no one gets any extra room, but everyone has a tray table wedged against his ribs and a stranger’s scalp five inches from his chin. It is a tiny, mechanical piece of selfishness. The airlines sell the same tight space twice over, and then leave the passengers to fight each other for the difference. A sensible man stays upright, not out of any saintly virtue, but because he knows that if he leans back he will only force the man behind him to do the same, and the whole cabin becomes a squalid staircase of tilted knees and jammed elbows. Yet almost everyone pushes the button. It gives a brief, false sense of mastery, like taking an inch of land in a crowd by putting your elbows out.

name: Virginia Woolf
essay: Let us step for a moment into this immaculate drawing room where no one ever sits down, but each person stands stiffly by the window holding out a crisp, white card. On it is written, in the neatest black ink, every dinner he has ever attended, every compliment paid to him by a magistrate, and the precise sum of his virtues. We watch him add another line with a gold pen, smiling at his neighbour, who is busy writing an equally glowing account of his own industrious habits. How extraordinary, we say, that anyone should wish to live in a house made entirely of glass shopfronts; yet here they all are, dusting their own busts, adjusting the light to catch their best profile. To admit to a failure of energy, or a Tuesday spent gazing out at the rain, would be to shatter the glass altogether. The air smells faint of varnish and freshly printed paper. One turns away from these radiant portraits of success and feels, against the palm, the cold, comforting handle of a wooden door leading out into the dark garden, where a cabbage leaf sways silently in the damp wind.

name: Douglas Adams
essay: The curious thing about being read to is that it was abolished, with great ceremony, at about the age of seven, on the grounds that one had learned to do it oneself, and has now been reinstated for adults on the grounds that they have not got the time. This is the real selling point. Nobody listens to a book because they want to hear it. They listen because the alternative was not reading it at all, and a person who has spent forty minutes on a motorway with a novel in the passenger seat feels, quite reasonably, that the book is now in some way in the car and the matter has been dealt with. The arrangement has a hidden flaw, which is that the book proceeds at the speed of a man in a studio, and not at the speed of the listener. A reader who encounters a dull paragraph skims it. A listener must sit through all of it while it is delivered, with perfect diction and unwavering sincerity, by someone who has been paid to find it fascinating and has done an excellent job. He also does the voices. Every character in the book is now somebody's impression of a person, and the heroine will sound like that for the rest of your life. Still, it is hard to condemn anything that has got a whole nation to finish a book while washing up. Whether they have read it is a question the dishes do not ask.

name: Nora Ephron
essay: I had my gallbladder out at New York Hospital on a Tuesday, and the last thing I remember is an anesthesiologist named Dr. Feldman asking me to count backward from ten. I got to eight. I had planned to get to one. I am a person who finishes things, who reads the last page of the ingredients list, and I was cheated. Nobody gets to seven. That is the great secret of the countdown: it is a test no one has ever passed, and they give it anyway. What I think about is not the cutting. It is the missing hour and forty minutes. Somebody opened me up, rummaged around, and sewed me shut, and I wasn't there. I was not asleep, because sleep has dreams and a lumpy mattress and a husband who steals the Pratesi sheets. This was nothing. I woke up in recovery, asking for a Diet Coke and a mirror, in that order. People say it's like death, and I suppose that's the point. They put you under, and you come back and complain about the hospital gown. I did. I complained for a week. It had a snap in exactly the wrong place. I have never once thanked Dr. Feldman. I don't know why. I think I was embarrassed that I got to eight.

name: Anthony Bourdain
essay: I have sent the thumbs-up to a man who had just told me his mother was in the hospital. Not proud of it. My thumb was faster than my conscience, and there it went, a little yellow fist of approval, off into the night with all the warmth of a rubber stamp at the DMV. That's the confession. Now the rest. The defense of these things is always the same: tone. Text is cold, they say, and the little faces put the heat back. Maybe. But I spent twenty years in kitchens where nobody had time for tone, and we managed to say everything. A cook who slams your pass with the flat of a sauté pan has told you his whole opinion of the fish. A look across the line at 9:40 on a Saturday carries a paragraph. That's language. It costs you something to produce. The crying-laughing face costs nothing. That's the problem. It is the garnish of the digital age: a sprig of parsley on every plate, whether the plate is a eulogy or a parking ticket. And like all garnish, it mostly exists to cover for the cook who had nothing to say. Say the thing. Or don't. But don't send me the little yellow guy.

name: Walt Whitman
essay: Went last evening to see the green ogre, and came out into the street a good deal cheer'd. Swamp, outhouse, onion, mud-bath, a pot of something boiling; then the castle, the lava, the drawbridge, the dragon chain'd up in her cellar of bones. All of it made out of numbers, I am told, by hundreds of young men and women at their desks, and yet the mud looks like mud, the ear-wax like ear-wax, the donkey's hide takes the light as a real hide does. The fairy people of the old books are turn'd out of their houses and driven into his bog--Pinocchio, three pigs, a gingerbread man, the wolf in the grandmother's nightcap, Robin Hood and his Merry Men doing Chinese kicks.
