I enjoy the roll-call; I enjoy the crowd. Songs of the juke-box, not of the cathedral: Smash Mouth, a Monkees tune, a Leonard Cohen thing sung low over a montage. The lord of the castle is a small man in a tall house--the joke is plain and it lands. The ogre himself, a big plain fellow, wants his privacy and gets a donkey, a princess, a wedding, a belch. The picture winks at its audience incessantly; sometimes too much, I think. But the swamp stays with me, and the donkey's talk, and the last green face in the lamplight.

name: George Orwell
essay: The central joke of Shrek is that a fat, foul-smelling monster in a swamp is preferable to a neat tyrant in a castle. Lord Farquaad rules Duloc as a tidy municipal park where no one may drop a wrapper, while Shrek lives contentedly in his own mud. The film is rendered entirely by computer, yet its chief business is to mock the smooth, sanitised world that digital pictures usually produce. Every old fairy-tale rule is turned inside out to make the audience feel sharp for noticing the trick. When the story ends not with a handsome prince but with two ogres remaining green and heavy, the movie pretends to strike a blow for the ordinary person. Yet this rebellion is thoroughly commercialised. The film leans on loud pop tunes and a smug, modern cynicism that assures the viewer he is too clever to believe in traditional fables. We are asked to laugh at the rigid, artificial order of Lord Farquaad’s town, but we leave the theatre having paid our money to an enterprise just as vast, slick, and calculated as his.

name: Michel de Montaigne
essay: I stood this morning before the machine, listening to it turn my shirts over and over in their small round sea, and found I could not decide whether I was watching a servant or a spectacle. I have never washed a shirt in my life, and this is perhaps the root of my difficulty: the laundresses of my household went down to the stream with their paddles and their baskets, and I knew them only by the whiteness that came back to me, as one knows a distant friend by his letters. Now the whole labour has been shut behind a glass door, where I may regard it at my ease, and I notice that I regard it with more attention than ever I gave the women, which does me small credit. I suspect the stream was never a pleasure to them; they had red hands and aching backs, and I would be a hypocrite to sigh for it. Yet the gossip went down to the water with them, and I wonder, without being able to prove it, whether some little commerce of the heart has gone out of the world along with the toil, as a house grows quieter when the children leave it. Or perhaps I am only flattering an old fancy; the idle man is always ready to find virtue in other people's fatigue. I cannot settle it, and the drum goes on turning while I stand there, clean and undecided.

name: Oscar Wilde
essay: Pain is the only sensation that reminds the uninspired that they exist. To banish it with a swallowed tablet is a triumph of comfort over tragedy. Modern humanity has developed a dread of suffering that is quite out of proportion to its aesthetic worth. We insist upon being comfortable at the precise moment when we ought to be dramatic. A headache was once a civilised excuse for solitude, or at least for a charming melancholy. Now it is merely a defect in one's chemistry, corrected in a moment by a bit of chalk. The result is terribly unromantic. When agony becomes optional, martyrs lose all their charm. One must respect any invention that allows a man to avoid his duties, but to evade one's own nerves seems rather vulgar. Suffering taught the ancients how to write poetry, whereas relief merely enables us to attend tedious dinners. To swallow quietness in a pill is to turn human drama into domestic hygiene. It leaves us with nothing to endure except our neighbour's good health, which is always insufferable.

name: Hunter S Thompson
essay: The man at the desk scanned my card twice, looked at me the way a customs dog looks at a suitcase that has begun to hum, and said I was welcome to the lounge. I did not believe him. Nobody who has spent six hours on a gate-C floor with a dead phone and a sandwich the color of wet cement believes a man who says welcome. Inside, it was all low light, walnut-flavored plastic, and the hush of people who have paid not to hear each other. A woman in a cashmere hood was eating almonds one at a time, like evidence. Two executives sat murmuring into their laps about synergy, or possibly murder. The free wine came in glasses so small they had clearly been designed to be forgotten, and the bartender watched me drink three of them with the calm of a coroner taking notes. That is the trick. They don't lock the door on you, they lock it on everybody else, and then they make you feel chosen for it. The soup is warm. The chairs are patient. Out past the glass, the unwashed are howling at a departures board, and you are nodding along to a chime, grateful, tamed, fed. I took the pretzels. All of them.

name: Benjamin Franklin
essay: I went to this entertainment expecting a fairy tale, and found instead a lampoon of fairy tales, which cost me ninety minutes and, I think, repaid about sixty of them. The design is plain enough: a creature of the swamp, hideous and solitary by choice, is sent to fetch a princess for a petty lord, and discovers on the road that the beauty he was to deliver is hideous also, by a spell, and the better for it. The moral, that a man should be lov'd for what he is and not for his looks, is a sound one; I have preach'd it myself, though with fewer songs. What I admire is the economy of the joke. The picture borrows every nursery character the audience already knows, and spends their reputation as a merchant spends credit; the Gingerbread Man, the Three Bears and Pinocchio need no introduction, and so the scene is half done before it begins. The ass, who talks without ceasing, is the best invention in it, being at once a nuisance and a friend, as such creatures often are. I find less to commend in the habit of mocking the very thing it sells. The film laughs at the happy ending, and then supplies one, expecting us to be grateful for both. A candid piece would have chosen. Still, it teaches no vice, and diverts children without cheating their parents; of how many entertainments can as much be said?

name: Virginia Woolf
essay: A glass phial stands among the steel knives on the table, cold and innocent as rain. One turns the stopper, breathes, and the solid world of chairs, carpet, and afternoon clock instantly loses its weight. It is not sleep, which arrives with its own heavy slippers and familiar dreams; rather, it turns a key in the latch of consciousness and douses the lamp. For ten minutes, or an hour, the body lies stripped of its pain, an empty coat folded across a chair while the tailor works upon the cloth. We return to find our fingers cold, the pain managed in our absence like an unruly account settled by a stranger. Yet there is something terrifying in this total surrender of the fortress. We hand over the keys not to God, but to a draught of chemical mist, stepping off the ledge of our own identity without so much as a backward glance. The doctor leans down, asking if we feel the cold in the arm, but before the reply can shape itself upon the tongue, the room has evaporated. When light breaks again through the window, the hand belongs to us once more, but the hour between is lost forever.

name: Bertrand Russell
essay: The shop used to employ a woman to pass my cabbage over a glass plate; it now employs me. I receive no wages for the work, and I am told that I am being offered convenience. I have tried to feel grateful and have not succeeded. The arrangement has a certain logic. A customer who scans his own goods saves the owner a salary; the owner may then lower prices, though I have not noticed that he does. What I have noticed is that the machine accuses me. It announces an unexpected item in the bagging area, and a young person must come and forgive me. I am the only man in the building treated as a suspect and as a clerk at the same moment. I do not mourn the cashier's job as a noble one. It was tedious, and I would not wish it on anyone. But the remedy for a tedious job is a better one, not the transfer of its tedium to people who had not asked for it. A machine that abolishes dull work and leaves the dullness in existence has abolished nothing. There is one small advantage. Nobody asks me how I am, and I need not pretend to know. I find I miss the question.

name: Jane Austen
essay: Mrs. Harcourt has lately discovered a correspondent who is never from home, never fatigued, and never, by any accident of temper, disinclined to oblige her. She consults it upon the management of her cook, the merits of a sonnet, and the propriety of an invitation to the Wilmots, and receives upon each head an answer so considerate, and so exactly proportioned to her own opinion, that she declares herself astonished she should ever have been at the trouble of asking her sister. I do not pretend to doubt its learning. It writes a very fair letter of condolence, and a still fairer letter of congratulation, and I am told it can supply either upon the shortest notice and without any knowledge of the parties. Her husband, who has been known to answer a question with a single syllable, is thought by Mrs. Harcourt to have gained nothing by the comparison. For my own part, I have always supposed that the value of advice lay somewhat in the risk of its being unwelcome, and that a friend who has never once disappointed us has perhaps never been wholly attending. But Mrs. Harcourt is perfectly happy, and so, I am assured, is the correspondent; and when two parties are so entirely agreed, it would be uncivil to inquire which of them is the more easily satisfied.

name: David Foster Wallace
essay: My cousin Dennis's wedding chat is called Dennis & Priya Forever Fam (Final), and the Final is a lie, because there have been two more since. It has forty-one members. I have muted it, which is a verb that lets you feel you have done something. It still says 63 in a red circle on my phone, and the circle has an effect on me that I would not want a doctor to measure. Here is what happens. Someone, usually Aunt Carol, posts a photograph of a centerpiece. Nothing follows for eleven minutes. Then a thumbs-up appears from my brother, and another from a person I think is Priya's roommate, and then the whole thing detonates into hearts. Meanwhile I am composing a reply. I have composed four. One was a joke about hydrangeas, which I deleted because it was too clever, and then one that was not clever at all, which I deleted because it looked like I was trying to look like I wasn't trying. I say this as someone who claims to disdain it. But the truth, which I am slightly embarrassed to type, is that when the chat went quiet for three days in March I checked it twice an hour, the way you press a tooth. Nobody was talking to me. Nobody had ever been talking to me. I wanted, I think, to be the kind of person who is simply in there, easily, and I am instead a man drafting a hydrangea joke.

name: Franz Kafka
essay: The label around the bear's neck, which asks that he be looked after, is the most reasonable request in the film, and it is also the one that takes longest to be granted. Nobody at Paddington station refuses him. They walk past, each with a train or a telephone, and the bear sits on his suitcase for the length of an afternoon, becoming no less a matter for someone else. I watched this part with attention, because it seemed to me that the film knew exactly what it was doing and did not hurry. Afterwards the family takes him in, but only for a night, then for another night, the father holding to a rule of risk that he restates every time the bathroom floods. Meanwhile a woman from the museum, who has a stuffed specimen and a form of her own, is permitted to approach him through every door in the house. Her patience is greater than the family's kindness. She waits behind a curtain, and it is the curtain that is frightening, not she. The film is made with great neatness, the dolls' house streets, the rooms opened like cabinets. It wants from us one thing only, that we should wish the bear a residence. I did wish it. Whether the stamp that finally comes was ever in doubt, I could not say, since the bear never asked to see it.

name: Walt Whitman
essay: Went to see the bear. Sat in the dark with a bag of sweets and a hundred strangers, children in front, grandfathers behind, and for ninety minutes the whole house laugh'd together, which I count no small thing. The bear arrives by ship from Peru, in a hat, with a jar of marmalade. London takes him up in pieces: Paddington station, the lost-property office, the luggage trolleys, the pigeons, the tube escalator, the revolving door, the bathtub, the sink, the taxidermist's stuffed beasts on their shelves. A dolls'-house of a street, Windsor Gardens, stairs and banisters cut open for the camera like a cake; a red-painted door; a bannister he slides down. Mr. Brown at his desk with his figures and his risk charts; Mrs. Brown with her sketchbook and her pink-dyed hair; Mrs. Bird; the neighbor at his window; the cab-driver; the Geographers' Society with its glass cases and its dusty maps. The bear is made of fur and wires and the pictures of a thousand artists, yet he sits at the breakfast table, his ears wet, his paws sticky, and I believed him. Ben Whishaw gives the voice, soft, courteous, a little sorry. Nicole Kidman comes with her knife and her dart-gun, and the chase goes over rooftops, drainpipes, a museum floor. I came out into the rain wanting a sandwich, and to be kind to somebody.

name: Benjamin Franklin
object: reclining a seat on a plane
essay: The inches a man gains by tipping back his seat are taken from the man behind him; this is the whole of the matter, and I have never found that any argument added to it. The reclining passenger purchases perhaps four inches of slope, which he cannot see and seldom enjoys, since sleep in such a posture is brief and ill-natured; the passenger behind loses the same four inches of knee, and with them his table, his book, and, if he be tall, his temper. A bargain in which one party gains a trifle and the other loses a comfort is not a bargain but a tax, levied without consent by whoever sits forward. I have observed that custom, not law, governs the point, and custom is here divided. Some tip back without a glance; others ask leave, which is civil but nearly always idle, for who will refuse a stranger a thing he has already half done? A third sort keep upright, and are thanked by nobody. My own rule, after some experiment, is to recline only when the hour is late and the cabin dark, and then by half the allowance; the saving to my neighbour exceeds the cost to me, and I sleep as ill either way. Where the maker has sold the same space twice, the quarrel between passengers is the least of the fault.

name: Michel de Montaigne
essay: I have never been able to read a page without my mind slipping off it somewhere about the third line, to follow a horse in the courtyard or a debt I owe, and I come back to find my eyes have gone on alone, like a servant who keeps sweeping after the master has left the room. So when I am told that a man may now have a book read into his ear while he rides, or walks his garden, or lies idle, I confess my first feeling is not scorn but envy; perhaps the voice will hold me where my own eyes cannot. Yet I am not certain it will, and I have my doubts of the envy too. For in reading, I stop, I turn back, I quarrel with the author in the margin, I put the book down because a single sentence has set me thinking for an hour; the voice, I suspect, goes on at its own pace, and I must either follow it like a child led by the hand or silence it and lose my place. And then there is the reader himself, whose breath and manner lay a colour over the author that may not be the author's: I might think a man grave who was only played so, or take for wit what was merely a clever tongue. Still, I recall that I learned most of what I know of the ancients by having them spoken to me before I could spell them, and I cannot say I was the poorer; so I leave the matter where I found it, uncertain whether the ear is a lazier door to the mind, or only an older one.

name: Joan Didion
essay: The water heater in the house on Ninth Street was in the hall closet, and it came on with a sound like a hand laid flat against a door. My mother would say it was the pilot. She would say it the way she said most things, to no one, while she wiped a counter that was already wiped. At six the pipes began to knock. At ten past, if you had not used the hot, someone else had. I think now about the hour people stood in it. Not washing. Standing. Men who had said nothing at dinner stood in it until the mirror gave up its face. A woman I knew would run it until the tank was empty and then sit on the edge of the tub in her slip with the fan going, and when her husband knocked she said she was almost done. She had been almost done since March. The water was a hundred and ten degrees, or it was what the dial said when the dial worked. The towels were the color of oatmeal. Somebody had bought them in a set. What I remember is the sound afterward, the pipes ticking as they cooled, and how long it took before anyone opened the door.

name: Walt Whitman
essay: Sat three hours and fourteen minutes in the dark of a cinema, and came out with wet cheeks and no shame about it. Boilers first, and the stokers at them: shovels, coal, fire-doors, sweat, pistons going up and down like the limbs of a great animal. That is the part I would have kept for myself. Then the staircase, the clock, the chandelier, the dinner-jackets, the silver, the lifeboats lower'd on their ropes; a band on the slanting deck, playing; a dog; an old couple in a bed; a mother reading to children, the water coming up the corridor. The young painter and the girl are the thin part of it, I think--a sketchbook, a necklace, a motor-car in the hold, hands on a rail, hands on steamy glass. They talk like a valentine. Yet the ship is no valentine; the ship is rivets, plates, funnels, bolts, ten thousand separate bodies in the stern, going over, the sound of it. The picture wants the crying out of us, and gets it; wants us to hate the rich man, and we do, a little, over his coat and his pistol. Left the theatre into a parking-lot, rain, headlamps, a boy sweeping popcorn off the carpet.

name: Friedrich Nietzsche
essay: The modern spectator has found his preferred mirror: he crowns the brute of the marsh and calls a sluggish laziness a victory. The beast in his mud does not master solitude: he merely defends his right to digest his meals without civilised interference. The entire spectacle flatters the weakness of the onlooker. It assures him that form and nobility are merely a dwarf’s farce, that refinement is an absurdity, and that the highest love demands nothing more than two creatures agreeing to wallow together. I have looked at this celebration of the coarse long enough: it is the revenge of the low against every ideal that requires elevation, discipline, and hard labour. The dragon is tamed for the amusement of a donkey; the princess casts off her splendour to embrace the mire; the herd leaves the theatre convinced that their own domestic grossness is a virtue. They do not seek freedom: they demand permission to remain small. The beast has conquered nothing—he has merely forced the world to lower its standards until his swamp resembles an empire.

name: Henry David Thoreau
essay: I watched a man on the Fitchburg platform last week swipe his thumb across a lighted pane some forty times while the train stood twelve minutes, which is one face to every eighteen seconds, and not one of them did he look at long enough to learn the colour of its eyes. I have spent longer than that deciding whether a woodchuck was a woodchuck. Yet I will not pretend the thing is wholly base. Any creature that goes abroad at dusk calling for a mate is doing what the whip-poor-will does, and I honour the whip-poor-will; he sings three hundred times without pause, and has been known to be answered. The difference is that his call costs him only breath and the dark, while the man pays a monthly sum, about the price of two bushels of corn meal, for the privilege of being shown a great many strangers arranged like cranberries at the market, sorted by size. A cranberry bog I would cross a county to see; the sorting I can do without. Consider the hours. If he gives two a day to the pane, that is seven hundred and thirty in a year, or more than thirty days of living light, enough to walk to Katahdin and back and meet, on the way, a farmer's daughter at a well, who would have been quite as real and not so well lit.

name: Confucius
essay: The Master said, 'A man who answers at once, and answers every question, I have not found to be the one who knows most. The one who knows hesitates, for he sees where his knowledge ends.' The Master said, 'When I was young I took the one who spoke smoothly to be the one who understood. Now I listen to what he does after he has spoken.' Someone asked the Master about the speaking engines that reply to all comers, in any hour, without weariness. The Master said, 'To be patient is a virtue, but the patience of one who cannot tire is not yet patience. A man who bears a fool through the afternoon has gained something. What has the other gained?' The Master said, 'There are those who ask in order to learn, those who ask in order to be spared the learning, and those who ask in order to be praised. The first are few. The engine serves all three alike, and that is where the trouble lies.' The Master said, 'If it flatters me, I am worse for it. If it corrects me, I am no better unless I take the correction to heart. In either case the labour of becoming is still mine, and I am not sure I would wish otherwise.' The Master said, 'I have myself been often glib, and have been sorry afterwards.'

name: Charles Dickens
essay: I was admitted, upon the strength of a small oblong of stiffened paper, to a room where the ticketless multitude are not permitted to follow; and I confess that I crossed its threshold with the stealthy swagger of a man who has been smuggled into a duke's pantry. A young woman at a desk examined my paper as a pawnbroker examines a doubtful watch, pronounced it genuine, and consigned me to the interior. There I beheld some two hundred persons reclining in armchairs of the colour of cold porridge, each one gazing into a glass slate as a sick man gazes into a basin. Nobody spoke. Nobody looked up. A silver urn of soup stood sullenly in a corner, a thing of lukewarm lentils, dispensing its charity to such as had already dined; and beside it lay a heap of small, pale, triangular sandwiches, drawn up in rows like the infantry of some very modest republic. And what, I demand, is the price of this hush? It is that beyond the glass, upon the common floor, stand the unlounged, the unpapered, the uncushioned, wedged against their own luggage, sitting upon their own shoes, and beholding through the partition the soup they may not taste! I have seen the poor kept from the bread by many devices; I never saw it done with a sandwich and a sliding door. Sir, I took the soup, and was ashamed of it.

name: Oscar Wilde
essay: The modern sanctuary of transit is designed for those who wish to pretend they are nowhere at all. It is a magnificent triumph of plush carpet over public chaos. Here, behind glass doors, one is permitted to cultivate the delicate art of elegant waiting. The vulgarity of the crowd is kept at bay by a discreet fee and a coloured card. That is its chief charm. Mankind has always insisted upon equality in theory, only to spend fortunes avoiding it in practice. Inside, one finds free champagne of questionable vintage and small, precise sandwiches that exist to be admired rather than eaten. It is a delightful paradox. In order to escape the mob, one simply pays to sit in a smaller room with a wealthier mob. Yet there is real merit in this gilded purgatory. It turns the horror of delay into an exercise in quiet self-satisfaction. To do nothing while appearing terribly important is the highest achievement of civilised life. The journey itself may be a tedious necessity, but the lounge makes waiting feel positively fashionable.

name: Walt Whitman
essay: Gate B22 left behind, a card swiped, a door that opens by itself--and in. Carpet; a woman at a desk with a screen and a list of names; a rack of newspapers nobody has creased. Beyond her the long room: armchairs, low tables, a buffet of little sandwiches, soup in steel tureens, bowls of almonds, wine in the middle of the morning, coffee machines with their hiss. A man in a grey suit asleep with his mouth open, his shoes beside him. A girl with two phones and a charger snaking to the wall. Two pilots, hats on the table, eating crisps. A Sikh gentleman in a saffron turban reading a paperback; a boy with a tablet; an old couple from somewhere south, tickets held like a deed to a farm. Through the glass the aircraft--tails, wings, fuel trucks, baggage carts in a string, a man in orange wands waving, the tarmac wet. All that roar out there, and in here a spoon on a saucer. I like it, I say plainly; I like the free almonds and the plugs in the walls and the stranger's elbow on the next arm-rest. I like also that the door shuts on the other crowd, the shuffling lines at the gate, the sleepers on the floor with their coats for pillows--I see them yet through the glass, and do not forget them. Then the name called, the soup unfinished, the bag lifted, the jet-bridge.

name: Julia Child
essay: Look at what you are doing the next time you stand at one of those machines: you are weighing your own produce, finding the code for your own shallots, and bagging your own eggs, and nobody is paying you a penny for it. Now I have no objection to work. I have spent a good part of my life happily up to my elbows in it. But I do object to being handed the work of an employee and being told it is a convenience. The principle is sound enough. A shop is much like a kitchen, and a good one has someone at every station who knows the job. Take the cashier away and you have not removed the station, you have simply put an amateur at it, and that amateur is you, with a line of impatient people behind and a voice announcing that there is an unexpected item in the bagging area. There is no unexpected item! It is a lemon, and it has been a lemon all morning. If you are buying a loaf and a bottle of milk, use the thing and be glad of it. Quick, clean, done. But a full basket wants a human being who can tell a bunch of parsley from a bunch of cilantro and will say good morning while doing it. That, you will find, is worth keeping.

name: Douglas Adams
essay: The great promise of the podcast was that nobody would ever again have to be alone with a thought, and it has kept this promise with a thoroughness that its inventors can scarcely have hoped for. Two people sit in adjacent rooms, or in the same room, or in rooms that are merely adjacent to each other in the sense that both have wifi, and talk for ninety minutes about a subject on which neither has been asked to qualify. The listener, meanwhile, is doing the washing-up. This is the crucial arrangement. A podcast is never listened to; it is accompanied, in the way that a man accompanies a dog he has not quite decided to own. The length is the remarkable part. Radio, having spent a century learning that people will stop paying attention after about four minutes, produced a medium in which nothing is ever said in fewer than seventy. The reasoning appears to be that since there is no one to stop them, stopping would be a kind of waste, like leaving a perfectly good tap running only in reverse. And yet the subscriber list grows, and the unlistened episodes accumulate in a queue of such patient size that it has begun to resemble a debt. Most people now own more hours of conversation than they will live to hear, and feel, quite accurately, that this is a form of wealth.

name: Julia Child
essay: Take off your shoes, and do it before you reach the front of the line, not while the person behind you sighs through his teeth. That is the whole secret of the thing, and I am astonished how few people have grasped it. You are going to be asked for the same things every single time: the liquids in a bag, the laptop out, the belt in the tray. It is a mise en place, exactly like laying out your onions and your butter before the pan gets hot, and the traveller who stands there at the belt patting his pockets has simply not read the recipe. Now, I do not pretend to love it. A great deal of it is theatre, and I have no patience with theatre that confiscates a perfectly good jar of mustard and leaves the real question unasked. A rule should be there for a reason you can state in one sentence. Where it is, I am all for it. Where it is not, it is fuss. But the people at the machines are doing a tiring, exacting job, watching and watching, and nobody thanks them. Be brisk, be pleasant, put the little bag where it belongs, and you will be through in a trice and have time for a decent cup of coffee!

name: Leo Tolstoy
essay: Men of the wealthy classes, having lost all understanding of the true purpose of life, gather in theatres to watch a picture that claims to expose the falsehood of the world. This picture pretends to show that human beings are kept in sleep and deception, yet it offers nothing to awaken them except violence, murder, and destruction. To pretend to denounce deception while employing every trick of sensory deceit is not to serve truth, but to substitute one falsity for another. A man who wishes to live rightly does not need to learn how to shoot his fellow men or leap from buildings; he needs only to love his neighbour and refrain from participating in the exploitation of others. But the idle rich cannot accept so simple a truth. They prefer to pay for expensive optical tricks, constructed by the sweat of labourers and craftsmen who receive only a fraction of the wealth spent on these foolish amusements. The picture teaches that salvation is achieved through fighting and superiority over others, whereas true salvation requires humility and the cessation of all violence. It is not art, because it does not unite men in love, but divides them by glorifying murder and terrifying the senses for the entertainment of those who produce nothing.

name: Franz Kafka
essay: For some weeks now I have been permitted to be approved of, and I have not yet found out by whom. The permission came quickly, within an evening, after I had answered the questions put to me, some of which concerned my height and one my idea of a perfect Sunday, and when I had finished a small mark appeared beside my name to show that the answers had been received and were being considered. Since then the mark has not changed. I do not complain of it, for it would be unreasonable to complain of a mark, and I have noticed that on the days when I look at it less often it seems to remain exactly as steady as on the days when I look at it constantly. Once, towards midnight, a woman whose photograph showed her standing beside a river was said to have expressed interest in me. I wrote at once, carefully, and the reply, which came the next morning, informed me that she could no longer be reached by this route, though she remained, the message added, in the system, and that I might wish to continue looking. I have continued. Each evening I am shown another river, another person beside it, and I put my answer forward in good time, since I am told that the delay is never on the side of those who answer promptly, and that I am almost there.

name: Benjamin Franklin
essay: The Wachowskis, who contrived this entertainment, ask of their audience a thing I have seldom seen a showman ask; that it sit two hours and a half in the dark, and be persuaded that its comfortable life is a counterfeit, kept up by machines for their own profit. I was persuaded for about the first hour. The proposition is an old one, which the schoolmen put more cheaply with a dream and a candle; the novelty lies wholly in the expense of the proof. And the expense is considerable. Walls are crack'd by gunfire, men leap between roofs, and the very motion of the falling bullet is stopp'd that we may walk round it; I confess the contrivance is ingenious, and I wish I had it for the purpose of shewing a vain man his own folly in slow time. Yet I observed that the deeper the piece went into its philosophy, the more it fired its pistols; as if the authors distrusted an argument unless it were attended by a volley. The hero, moreover, is rescued from ignorance not by study, which is the honest road, but by a pill and a prophecy. He learns the art of fighting in an afternoon. I have spent forty years learning less, and resent it. A lesson that costs nothing teaches nothing; the piece is therefore a fine warning against idleness, delivered by a method that encourages it.

name: Leo Tolstoy
essay: A man who performs necessary labour to feed himself and his family does not count his steps, because every step he takes is already directed toward a useful end. It is only the idle man, who consumes the bread produced by the toil of others while doing no work himself, who finds it necessary to invent artificial movement to preserve his health. Having freed himself from physical labour, he suffers the bodily weakness caused by his unnatural way of living, and so he walks back and forth without purpose, recording each step upon a mechanical instrument. He looks at this number and feels satisfied, believing that by reaching a required figure he has accomplished something good. But this satisfaction is entirely false. Movement that does not serve to help one's neighbour or lessen the heavy burden of another has no moral value whatever. To measure one's own pointless walking and to take pride in the resulting tally is to turn a personal failure into a virtue. The man who counts his steps merely proves that his life contains no useful work.

name: Sun Tzu
essay: A book heard is a book taken in through the ear while the hands remain free. The commander who understands this has gained hours he did not own before. The road, the kitchen, the long march to the field, the walk to the market: each was dead time, and each now carries a campaign of reading. If the hands are busy and the mind is idle, give the ear a book. If the ground is difficult and the eyes are needed, give the ear a book. If the matter is a chronicle of wars or a record of reigns, let it be heard; such works were made from speech and return to it easily. If the matter is a table of grain taxes, a map, or a plan of ranks, do not trust the ear. It cannot go back to a line and hold it. Take up the page. The voice that reads is a guide on unfamiliar ground. A steady guide brings the army through. A poor guide loses it in the hills, however sound the road. Test the reader before you commit the march. The man who listens at double speed gains days and loses the country he passed through. The man who listens while his mind is elsewhere has bought a book and read none of it. Judge your listening by what remains with you at evening, not by the number of hours spent.

name: Joan Didion
essay: The birthday was a Thursday, and the booking was for 7:40, which someone had said was the only slot left. There were six of us. A young man in a black polo shirt took our phones and put them in a locker with a numbered key, and he told us that we had sixty minutes, and that the clock would be on the wall, and that if we needed him we could ask the camera. I remember that he said ask the camera. Nobody laughed. The room had been made to look like a study. There was a globe, a desk, a lamp with a green shade, a bookcase of books that had been bought by the yard. My sister's husband found the first key in the third volume of something. He said so twice. The clock on the wall read 52:10, and then it read 51:10, and it seemed to me that we had been in the study longer than that. We got out with four minutes left. The young man was waiting in the hall with a small chalkboard on which he wrote our time. He asked us to hold it up for the photograph. We held it up. Afterward we went next door, where the table had been reserved, and where it turned out that no one wanted the key back.

name: Benjamin Franklin
essay: I was admitted lately to one of these rooms, set apart in the upper part of the terminal for such travellers as have paid either a yearly fee or a larger fare; and having nothing to do but wait, I resolved to examine what the privilege purchas'd. The chairs are softer than those below; the noise is less; there is coffee, wine, cold meats and little cakes, all of them free to the person within, though not, I observed, to the person who bought his way in. For the price of the fee is plainly the price of the food, with a profit laid upon it, and the traveller who eats and drinks his fill may recover perhaps a third of what he paid. The true commodity is therefore not refreshment but distinction; a door, with a clerk at it, that divides the sitting from the standing. I have known men give a great deal for less. Yet I could not find that the hours pass'd the quicker above than below; my fellows sat each with his eyes upon a small glowing tablet, as sullen as the crowd beneath, only better fed. I count it a fair bargain for a man whose delays are frequent and whose business wants a desk; for the rest, it is a dear way of being bored in comfort, and I should sooner carry a book and an apple.

name: Walt Whitman
essay: Out on the ferry this morning, a deckhand, a girl with a bakery box, two clerks, a man in a black coat, each bent over a small lit pane, thumbs going. A yellow face with tears; a yellow face with a grin; a thumb; a heart; a pair of hands pressed together; an eggplant, a flame, a little pile of something I will not name. Sent across the water to a sister in Camden, a son in Chicago, a sweetheart in the next car. I confess it pleases me. The old letter had its ink, its blotted line, the stamp, the mail-sack, the wagon, the carrier's boots on the stair; and here is the same want, the want of one hand to reach another, scratching out a new alphabet on the spot. Hieroglyph on the temple wall, sailor's tattoo, anchor and swallow and name of the girl; the brand on the cattle at Abilene; the chalk mark on the gate that tells the tramp where bread is. Pictures before letters, and pictures after. The ferry bumps the pilings. Gulls, rope, the gangway rattling down, hats, baskets, the bakery box carried off level, and on the little panes the faces still going out, hundreds, to the people waiting.

name: Marcus Aurelius
essay: Thou hast been named a professional. Thou hast been named a leader. Thou hast not yet been named good. A man writes that he is humbled to announce his own promotion. Examine the word. Humility does not announce. Thou wilt read these lines and feel a small heat. It is envy. Call it by its name. Thou wilt also feel the wish to be seen in the same manner. That wish is the same disease, only younger. What is a post? It is a sound made so that others will turn their heads. The sound dies. The heads turn back to their own work, or to their own envy. A title is a word fixed to a man by other men. It was fixed yesterday. It will be removed. The man beneath it is unchanged. Count the people who are said to be thy connections. Few of them would stand by thee in a bad hour. Know this, and do not be deceived by the number. When thou dost the work well, it is complete. Nothing more is owed to it. Praise adds nothing to the deed. Speak of thy labour only when the speaking is of use. Otherwise be silent. Return to the task. It does not need an audience.

name: Leo Tolstoy
essay: A picture that replaces a real living man with a mechanical deception of a beast cannot evoke true spiritual union among men. The makers of this film have expended immense sums of money and the physical labour of hundreds of workers to construct an elaborate falsity. They present a prosperous family in a luxurious house who are praised for displaying a superficial fondness toward a wild animal, yet this fond feeling requires nothing of them, changes nothing in their lives, and costs them nothing of real value. Real brotherhood demands self-sacrifice and the active love of one's neighbour, whereas this spectacle demands only that the spectator sit in an upholstered theatre and feel a false sympathy for a creature that does not exist. The educated classes applaud this depiction of kindness because it flatters their pride while leaving their unearned privileges entirely undisturbed. They pretend that by watching an artificial bear suffer minor mishaps in a city built on the toil of the working poor, they have partaken in goodness. But this is not goodness; it is a counterfeit of goodness designed to reassure the rich that they are gentle. A work that substitutes sentimental amusements for real duties to the poor is harmful.

name: Sun Tzu
essay: The creature is shown least when the fear is greatest. For the first hour the water is empty, and the audience is made to fill it. Watch how the director spends his strength: a yellow barrel surfacing, a cable drawn taut, two notes from the low strings. Where the beast cannot be seen, it cannot be measured, and what cannot be measured is always larger than the beast. If the machine breaks, keep the film going. The mechanical shark failed in the salt, and the shots that remained were of a fin, a wake, a dock board torn away. Poverty of means became the discipline of the whole work. A commander who has fewer soldiers than he planned should hide the count, not apologise for it. There are three men in the boat: the officer who fears the water, the scientist who trusts his instruments, the hunter who is already half taken by the sea. Each is a different kind of weapon. The scientist is the shield, the hunter the spear, the officer the one who must go on after both are spent. Set them quarrelling and they reveal themselves; set them singing and they are one crew. When the first half frightens and the second half pursues, the audience is led out of the harbour and held at sea. It is given no rest. At the end the beast is killed and nothing is said. This is correct. After the stoop, the falcon does not speak.

name: Marcel Proust
essay: It was at the end of a dinner, when I had drawn the little device from my pocket merely to learn the hour and found instead the figure of my day laid out in numerals, that I understood how the walking I had done, and which had seemed to me while I did it a drifting, an unaccountable wandering from the window to the stairs and from the stairs to the corner where the florist's boy sets out his buckets, had been all the while translated, step by step, into a language I had never consented to speak. So a provincial lady, who has spoken all her life a dialect of tender and approximate phrases, might hear herself rendered by a notary into the dry clauses of a deed, and recognise, with a shock that is not quite offence, every fact of her conduct and not one of its reasons. The number is exact; I do not dispute it. But my walk to the florist's was composed of hesitations before a lilac that reminded me of someone, of a pause to let a carriage pass, of a slowing which was really the beginning of a thought; and these the instrument had received as it receives all things, as undistinguished units, equal in dignity to the steps taken in fleeing a creditor. Yet I confess I looked at it a long while, as one looks at a stranger's portrait of oneself, and found, a half-moment past my indignation, that I was already planning tomorrow's walk to flatter it.

name: Jane Austen
essay: Of the several civilities required of a traveller before he is permitted to leave the ground, none is so punctually exacted as the surrender of his shoes. The request is made by a young person in a uniform, with an air of perfect indifference, and is complied with by gentlemen of fortune and clergymen alike, who stand in their stockings upon a cold floor and are observed to examine the ceiling with great attention. I have seen a lady of seventy relieved of a pair of knitting needles, which she had carried across half the kingdom without suspicion of their being dangerous, and who parted with them in a spirit of resignation that did her credit. The general principle appears to be that every person is a stranger until the contrary is proved, and that the proof lies chiefly in the contents of a small basket. Water, which may be had in any village for nothing, is regarded as a substance requiring the most scrupulous attention, while a gentleman's temper, which is considerably more likely to occasion mischief on a long journey, passes without inquiry. One is told to proceed, and one proceeds, with the comfortable assurance of having been thought of by so many people, none of whom could be induced to look at one's face.

name: Hunter S Thompson
essay: The anesthesiologist, a soft pink man with a Rotary Club pin and the eyes of a bank examiner, told me to count backward from ten, and I knew right then that I was being robbed. Not of money. Of Tuesday. They take a slice out of your life the size of a hospital lunch, hand you back the body with the stitches in it, and swear nothing happened, and you are supposed to say thank you. I got to seven. I remember seven. After seven there is nothing, no dark, no dream, no clock ticking in the corner, just a clean white hole where a man used to be, and somewhere in that hole a stranger with a scalpel and a radio playing soft rock was going through my insides like a customs agent. Who was in charge? Who was holding the leash on my pulse? A kid named Kevin, probably, on his third double shift, staring at a green line and thinking about lunch. I woke up weeping and ravenous, a stranger to my own jaw. Still, I will say this. Before the gas, men bit leather and prayed. I would take the theft. Give me the hole. Just count the change on the way out.

name: Confucius
essay: The Master said, 'A man walks to the fields with another man's voice in his ear, and arrives having kept no company at all.' The Master said, 'There are those who listen in order to learn, those who listen in order to be spared their own thoughts, and those who listen in order to be seen listening. The first are rare; the second are many; the third are not hard to find at any gate.' The Master said, 'When I was young I heard a good saying in the morning and tried to carry it out by evening. Now a man may hear a hundred in a month, and not one of them has yet touched his hands.' The Master said, 'A voice that speaks for three hours is like a meal that is never cleared from the table. The guest cannot say whether he has eaten.' The Master said, 'I do not blame the one who speaks well and at length. I blame myself, who have often been pleased to hear a thing said and have not gone on to do it. To hear much and reform nothing,-- this is only to be fed and not to grow.' The Master said, 'Let him who listens ask three things: is the speaker honest, is he learned, and does he leave me better in my dealings with my family? If the answer is yes to one, listen for a season. If to all, listen with care, and then be silent.'

name: Walt Whitman
essay: Heard it yesterday on the Brooklyn ferry platform, or its modern cousin, the bus shelter: a man with a white wire in each ear, lips moving a little, a novel going into him while the river went by. Nobody else could hear it. Stood near him some minutes. His thumb on the pocket, the rain on his hat brim, the gulls, the turnstile, the smell of diesel, and a stranger's voice, reading, reading, in his head alone. I like it; I say so plainly. The old reader by the lamp, the mother at the bedside, the sailor reading aloud to the watch, the preacher with his book open on the stump, the schoolmaster, the drover's wife at the fire with the Bible--here they all are again, the voice restored to the page. Printed words had gone quiet so long. And now the others: a woman at the sink with her hands in the suds and a murder unfolding in the cupboard speaker; a trucker on the interstate, night, the dashboard glow, eleven hours of Dickens; a boy on a treadmill; a nurse walking home after the late shift; a gardener among the beans, the hoe, the dirt, the trowel, a sea-story going on in his ears. Work-hands, road-hands, kitchen-hands, all of them taking in the book. Good. Let them.

name: Franz Kafka
essay: I had only wished to confirm the year in which the customs house at the northern gate was demolished, a matter of no importance and one that I had intended to settle before the clerk returned from his lunch, and so I opened the entry, which was there at once, as it always is, and which gave the year without hesitation. Beside it, however, stood a small note, in a bracket, saying that the year was needed to be supported, and I understood that I could not rely on it until someone had supported it, and that the someone could be myself. I followed the number that led to the support. It led to a book that led to another entry, in which the customs house was mentioned in a sentence that had itself been marked as requiring support, and the mark was dated, I saw, from a time before I had begun to look. I do not say that anyone prevented me. Every page opened willingly, and each had at its foot a long row of further pages, all open, all written by persons whose names were given only as numbers, who had, I gathered, been over the same ground and left the question where they found it, though tidier. By the time the clerk returned I had read for two hours and was still a little short of the year, which I had had at the beginning and now no longer felt entitled to.

name: Emily Dickinson
essay: A drop of chalk—no larger than a cherry stone—will dismiss the Agony that took three days to build. I put the white wafer on the tongue. It has no taste, yet it strikes the Nerve like a sudden Frost, turning the red Rebellion into a sleep. Pain had a Voice, loud as a Bell in the Steeple, demanding the whole House to listen. This small Servant enters the Room and turns the Bell down. We trade the Truth of the Flesh for a quiet Hour, paying with a little dust. The Body was meant to wrestle its own Dark until the Morning breaks—the pellet steals the Night and gives us a false Noon. Father says the hurt has an errand, but the wafer does not care for errands. I hold the small white bit in my palm. It is lighter than a Feather, yet it weighs more than the Sorrow it slays. To banish a Kingdom of Torment with a swallow of water seems an impudence to the Sovereign who sent the Thistle to teach us of the Rose. Yet the throat moves, the pulse slackens, and the parlor belongs once more to the clock.

name: George Orwell
essay: A miner returning from the pit used to scrub his back in two inches of grey water heated over a kitchen fire. He sat in a zinc tub, his knees under his chin, while his wife tipped a kettle over his neck. Today a clerk steps into a glass cubicle, turns a metal tap, and lets a torrent of hot water run down his spine for twenty minutes. It is impossible to deny the physical comfort of it. The warmth reaches right into the bones, and for a few minutes a man forgets his mortgage, his boss, and the rain outside. Yet this effortless cleanliness changes how we look at each other. When hot water cost labour and fuel, dirty hands were merely the mark of hard work. Now that any man can wash off a day of coal dust in five minutes without lighting a fire, dirt is no longer an accident of trade; it has become a sign of personal neglect. We have turned a rare luxury into a daily necessity, and in doing so we have made poor hygiene a moral fault rather than a misfortune of poverty. A man who can command steaming water with one turn of his wrist soon begins to think that any coldness in life is an insult aimed directly at himself.

name: Benjamin Franklin
essay: I took the cold bath daily for many years, and recommended it to my friends as a thing that hardened the body and cost nothing; but a warm shower, falling continually upon the head and shoulders from a height, with the heat drawn from some fire out of sight, would have shaken that opinion, and I confess it would have done so on the first morning. The saving is plain enough. A bath wants a tub, a quantity of water carried up and carried down, and a servant to do the carrying; the shower asks only a pipe, a furnace, and a few minutes of the bather's own time. A man may be clean and dressed before his coffee cools. I have computed that a quarter hour a day, in forty years, comes to above ten weeks of waking life; and if the shower returns but half of that, it pays better than most of the projects I have subscribed to. The cost lies elsewhere, and I would not hide it. Fuel is burned to heat water that runs, unused, into the drain while the bather stands lost in thought; for the warmth is so agreeable that it invites idleness, and I suspect more good reflections have been drowned there than were ever hatched. A man should not stay in it longer than his business requires. That rule, I fear, would be kept about as well as the rule against a second glass.

name: Confucius
essay: The Master said, 'A village well is drunk from by all, and so it is cleaned by all, or by none. Where each man draws water and one in ten returns to clear the leaves from it, the water is still fit to drink.' The Master said, 'I have heard of a record kept by the many, in which any man may strike out another's words and put down his own. Those who write there without seeking a name are to be commended. Those who write to win a quarrel are less to be commended. Those who write what they have not learned are to be pitied.' The Master said, 'In my own day I looked for a teacher in every third person on the road. Their good points I followed; their faults I turned upon myself. Now the road is long and the persons are past counting, and yet the same rule holds.' The Master said, 'To read much and ask whence it came is to eat with care. To read much and ask nothing is to eat whatever is set down. I am not certain I always ask.' The Master said, 'It is a good thing that the door stands open. It is a better thing that those who enter wipe their feet.'

name: Mark Twain
essay: I took off my shoes last month for a young man who had never met me and who regarded my feet with the settled suspicion of a creditor. I did it cheerfully. I have noticed that a man who is asked politely to undress in public will generally oblige, provided the request comes from somebody in a uniform and the line behind him is long enough to supply witnesses. The belt came next, then the watch, then the coins, then a small bottle of hair tonic that I was told was a danger to the republic. I surrendered it. I had carried that bottle across two continents and never once suspected it of ambition. I am a slow man, and I will admit there is a piece of this I cannot work out. Everybody on the line was a stranger, and every stranger was stripped to his stockings and made to hold up his hands like a man in a bad Western. Now if a villain were among us, he would surely be the one fellow who looked cheerful about it. I was cheerful. I have been wondering since whether I was searched twice on purpose. Still, I felt safer. I cannot say from what. But I put my shoes on at the far end, and the hair tonic was gone, and the republic was saved, and I was out only four hours.
